title: Inside a cell: the skin, the jelly and the instruction room

summary.text: A potato strip dropped in plain water stays stiff. The same strip in strong salt water goes floppy, though nobody squeezed it. Every potato cell has a thin skin, and water moves through that skin in both directions. Your child tests this with a fair test, then finds the three main parts of a cell, the membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus. They see how plant cells and animal cells differ, why cells are so small, and how one cell on her own can eat, move and sense. They learn how scientists proved the skin was there long before anyone could see it, and what nobody yet knows about the very first cell.
summary.art: Two potato strips held side by side: one stiff and straight from a cup of plain water, the other drooping over a finger from a cup of salty water.

intro.hook: Look at a bunch of coriander that has gone limp on the kitchen counter. Put the stems in a glass of water for an hour. The leaves stand up again. The water went in through the cut ends and the roots, but the leaves are far away. How did the water get to every leaf, and why did the leaves go floppy in the first place?
intro.text: Every leaf is made of tiny cells, and each cell has a thin skin. When a cell holds plenty of water, she is firm, and the leaf stands up. When she loses water, she goes soft, and the leaf droops. In this unit you find out what a cell is made of, what the skin does, and where the water goes. You also meet cells that live alone in a drop of pond water and do everything a body does.
intro.art: A limp coriander bunch on the left and the same bunch standing straight in a steel tumbler of water on the right, with a zoomed-in circle showing round, full cells in the standing leaf.

outcomes: I can name the three main parts of a cell, the membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus, and say what each one does.
I can say how plant cells and animal cells are alike and how they differ: cell wall, chloroplasts and a big vacuole.
I can explain that a cell's skin lets some things through and keeps others out, and that water moves through it in both directions.
I can run a fair test with potato strips in plain and salty water, and explain the result.
I can give examples of single-celled living things and say how one cell eats, moves, senses and gets rid of waste.
I can explain why cells stay small, using the idea of surface.
I can tell how scientists found the cell's skin before they could see it.
I can say that mitochondria and chloroplasts began as bacteria, and name what nobody knows yet about the first cells.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of a living thing that is alive on its own. Your body, a mango tree and a mushroom are all made of cells.
terms.example: A single drop of pond water can hold hundreds of single cells swimming about.
terms.art: A drop of water on a fingertip with a zoomed-in circle showing several swimming cells.

terms.meaning: The thin skin around a cell. It lets some things in and out and keeps other things away.
terms.example: Water passes through the membrane of a potato cell, but a grain of starch cannot.
terms.art: A round cell cut open, with the thin outer line coloured bright and small arrows crossing it.

terms.meaning: The jelly-like liquid that fills a cell inside the membrane. Most of the cell's work happens here.
terms.example: Under a microscope, the cytoplasm of a water-plant cell can be seen slowly flowing round and round.
terms.art: A cell with its inside shaded pale yellow and small arrows showing the jelly flowing in a circle.

terms.meaning: The round part of many cells that holds the instructions for building and running the cell. The instructions are written in DNA.
terms.example: A human skin cell has a nucleus. A bacterium does not.
terms.art: A cell with a large round nucleus in the middle and thread-like DNA drawn inside it.

terms.meaning: A small part inside a cell that has its own job, like a room in a house.
terms.example: The nucleus, the chloroplasts and the mitochondria are organelles.
terms.art: A cell drawn as a house with rooms, each room labelled with a small part.

terms.meaning: A stiff outer layer around the membrane of plant cells, fungus cells and bacteria. Animal cells do not have one.
terms.example: The cell walls of a cucumber make it crisp when you bite it.
terms.art: A square plant cell with a thick wall outside a thin membrane, beside a round animal cell with only a membrane.

terms.meaning: A green part inside plant cells that catches sunlight and uses it to make sugar.
terms.example: The green colour of a leaf comes from the chloroplasts inside its cells.
terms.art: A leaf cell packed with small green oval chloroplasts, with a sunbeam falling on it.

terms.meaning: A bag inside a cell that stores water and other things. A plant cell has one big vacuole that pushes against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm.
terms.example: A fresh celery stalk is crisp because the big vacuoles in its cells are full of water.
terms.art: A plant cell with a large pale blue vacuole filling most of the space and pressing on the wall.

terms.meaning: A small part inside most cells that releases energy from food. More than one are called mitochondria.
terms.example: A muscle cell that works hard has thousands of mitochondria.
terms.art: A cell with several bean-shaped mitochondria, each with folds inside, and a spark of energy leaving one.

terms.meaning: The movement of water through a membrane towards the side that has more dissolved stuff, such as salt or sugar.
terms.example: Water leaves a potato strip and goes into strong salt water, so the strip goes floppy.
terms.art: Two sides of a membrane: plain water on the left, salty water on the right, and arrows showing water moving towards the salty side.

terms.meaning: A living being whose whole body is one cell. She eats, moves, senses and makes more of herself, all with that one cell.
terms.example: An amoeba, a paramecium and a yeast are each a single cell.
terms.art: A pond-water drop showing an amoeba, a paramecium and a green euglena, each in a different shape.

terms.meaning: A single-celled living being with no nucleus. Her instructions float in the cytoplasm. More than one are called bacteria.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are a few thousandths of a millimetre long.
terms.art: A rod-shaped bacterium cut open, with a loop of DNA floating in the cytoplasm and no round nucleus.

terms.meaning: A single-celled living being that has no fixed shape. She pushes out a part of herself to move, and wraps herself around food to eat it.
terms.example: An amoeba in pond water wraps round a tiny green alga and takes it in.
terms.art: An amoeba with a blunt arm pushed out, curling round a small green cell.

terms.meaning: A single-celled living being shaped like a slipper, covered in tiny hairs that beat to push her through the water.
terms.example: A paramecium can swim many times her own length in one second.
terms.art: A slipper-shaped cell covered in short hairs, with a swirl showing her swimming forward.

terms.meaning: A single-celled living being that has green chloroplasts like a plant and swims with a whip-like tail like an animal.
terms.example: A green euglena swims towards light and makes sugar from sunlight.
terms.art: A long green cell with one waving tail at the front and a red spot that senses light.

terms.meaning: One thousandth of a millimetre. Cells are measured in micrometres.
terms.example: A human red blood cell is about 8 micrometres wide, so about 125 of them in a row would stretch across 1 millimetre.
terms.art: A millimetre ruler with a tiny zoomed-in section showing a row of small red cells laid end to end.

explanations.concept: The three main parts of a cell: skin, jelly and instruction room
explanations.definition: Almost every cell has a cell membrane around the outside, cytoplasm filling the inside, and DNA that holds the instructions. In many cells the DNA is kept inside a nucleus.
explanations.description: Think of a cell as a very small kitchen. The membrane is the wall and door of the kitchen. It decides what comes in and what goes out. The cytoplasm is everything inside the kitchen, the air and the counters. It is a jelly that is mostly water, and most of the cell's work happens in it. The nucleus is a locked cupboard that holds the recipe book. The recipe book is DNA. It tells the cell which things to build and when. Plant, animal and fungus cells have a nucleus. Bacteria do not. Their DNA floats loose in the cytoplasm. The kitchen picture is only a help. A real cell is not a still room. Everything in her is moving all the time.
examples: A cheek cell has a membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
A bacterium has a membrane and cytoplasm, and a loop of DNA floating loose in the cytoplasm with no nucleus.
A mature human red blood cell has lost her nucleus. She carries oxygen for about four months with no nucleus at all.
explanations.art: A cell drawn as a tiny kitchen: a wall with a small door as the membrane, the room inside as the cytoplasm, and a locked cupboard holding a recipe book as the nucleus.

explanations.concept: The cell membrane: a skin that chooses what passes
explanations.definition: The cell membrane is a thin layer of fatty molecules with proteins set into it. It lets some substances pass freely, helps some through special channels and pumps, and blocks the rest.
explanations.description: The membrane is about ten thousand times thinner than a hair. It is made of fat molecules that lie side by side in two layers. Each molecule has a head that likes water and a tail that hates water. In water, they turn the tails inward and the heads outward on their own, and make a thin sheet. Tiny molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide slip straight between the fat molecules. Sugar and many other things are too big or too charged, so special proteins in the membrane carry them across. Some proteins are pumps. A pump pushes things across against the way they would naturally go, and it uses energy to do so. A large part of the energy a cell spends goes into pumps. Water passes through the membrane slowly on its own, and much faster through water channels. The membrane is not a still wall. The fat molecules slide around each other like a very thin oil, and the proteins float in it.
examples: Oxygen passes through the membranes of your lung cells and into your blood.
Sugar from your food gets into your cells only with the help of carrier proteins.
A starch grain is far too big to pass through, so your body first cuts starch into sugar.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in slice of the membrane: two rows of fat molecules with round heads and wavy tails, a protein channel passing through, and small molecules crossing at different spots.

explanations.concept: Osmosis: water moves towards the saltier side
explanations.definition: Osmosis is the movement of water through a membrane from the side with less dissolved stuff to the side with more dissolved stuff.
explanations.description: Water molecules are always moving, and they pass back and forth through the cell membrane both ways. When there is more dissolved stuff on one side, such as salt or sugar, more water ends up on that side. In plain water, a potato cell has more dissolved stuff inside than outside. So water moves in, and the cell grows firm. In strong salt water, there is more dissolved stuff outside, so water moves out. The cell loses water and goes limp. This is why salt draws water out of mango pieces in pickle, and why a raisin swells in water. The salt does not suck on the water. Water simply moves through the membrane both ways, and more of it ends up on the side with more dissolved stuff. Osmosis happens at every skin. A cell can change how much dissolved stuff she keeps inside.
examples: Salt sprinkled on cut brinjal slices draws water out and leaves a wet plate.
Raisins left in water overnight swell, because their sugary insides draw water in.
A paramecium living in pond water has water flowing into her all the time, and she pumps it out again.
explanations.art: Two potato cells side by side: one in plain water, round and full with arrows pointing in, and one in salty water, shrunken with arrows pointing out.

explanations.concept: Cytoplasm: where the cell's work happens
explanations.definition: Cytoplasm is everything inside the cell membrane apart from the nucleus. It is a jelly made mostly of water, with the organelles floating in it.
explanations.description: Most of the chemistry of life goes on in the cytoplasm. Food is broken down, parts are built and waste is made. Tiny molecules zip around it, and larger parts are carried along on thin threads. In some cells, such as the cells of a pond plant called Hydrilla, the whole cytoplasm flows round the cell in a slow stream. This is called cytoplasmic streaming. It moves food and organelles around the cell. The cytoplasm is crowded. Proteins and other big molecules fill the space, so the jelly is thicker than the water you drink. Organelles float in it. The mitochondria release energy from food. In plant cells, the chloroplasts make sugar from sunlight.
examples: Look at a Hydrilla leaf under a good microscope and the green chloroplasts are carried around the cell by the streaming cytoplasm.
A raw egg yolk is one huge cell, packed with food for a chick.
When a red blood cell squeezes through a very narrow tube, her cytoplasm lets her bend and fold.
explanations.art: A plant cell with small arrows showing the cytoplasm flowing round the edge and carrying green chloroplasts along with it.

explanations.concept: The nucleus: the room that keeps the instructions
explanations.definition: The nucleus is a round organelle surrounded by its own double membrane. It holds the cell's DNA, which carries the instructions for building and running the cell.
explanations.description: Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist, named the nucleus in 1831 while looking at orchid cells. The nucleus keeps the DNA safe and organised. DNA is a very long molecule, and one human cell holds about two metres of it, folded up tightly inside a nucleus only a few thousandths of a millimetre across. The DNA is not a boss giving orders. It is more like a library. The cell copies out the pages she needs, and takes the copies out to the cytoplasm, where parts are built from them. Different cells use different pages. A skin cell and a nerve cell in the same body have the same DNA, but they read different pages. Before a cell divides, she copies all her DNA, so that each new cell gets a full set.
examples: A muscle cell and a skin cell in the same person hold the same DNA, but they use different parts of it.
Plant cells, animal cells and fungus cells all have a nucleus.
Bacteria keep their DNA in a loop in the cytoplasm, with no nucleus.
explanations.art: A nucleus drawn as a round room with a thick door, holding a library shelf, and a thin copied page being carried out through the door.

explanations.concept: Plant cells and animal cells: alike in most ways, different in three
explanations.definition: Plant cells and animal cells both have a membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus and mitochondria. Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
explanations.description: A plant cell has three extra things. The cell wall is a stiff layer outside the membrane. It is made of a tough material called cellulose, and it gives the cell her box-like shape. The chloroplasts catch sunlight and make sugar, which is why leaves are green. The large vacuole is a bag of watery liquid that takes up most of the cell and presses against the wall. Animal cells have no wall, so they can be many shapes: round, flat, long or spidery. Nerve cells are long and branched. Red blood cells are discs. The animal cell has small vacuoles instead of one big one. But the list is not as neat as it sounds. Fungi have cell walls but no chloroplasts. Bacteria have cell walls too. Plants and animals both have mitochondria, so a plant also releases energy from food, all day and all night.
examples: A cell from a leaf is box-shaped and has a wall, many chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
A cheek cell is a flat, irregular shape with no wall and no chloroplasts.
A mushroom cell has a wall, but no chloroplasts, because mushrooms do not make food from sunlight.
explanations.art: A box-shaped plant cell with a wall, chloroplasts and a big blue vacuole beside a roundish animal cell with a nucleus and tiny vacuoles, with the three plant-only parts circled.

explanations.concept: Why a plant stands up: cells full of water
explanations.definition: A plant stands up because the large vacuole in each of her cells is full of water that pushes against the stiff cell wall. This push is called turgor pressure.
explanations.description: A balloon inside a shoebox is a good picture. The balloon is the vacuole. The box is the cell wall. Fill the balloon with water and it pushes against the box and makes it firm. A plant that has plenty of water has cells that are all firm like this, and the stem and leaves stand up. When the plant loses more water than she takes in, the vacuoles shrink and pull away from the walls. The cells go soft, and the plant wilts. Water brings her back. A plant also moves by changing how much water is in certain cells. The touch-me-not plant, Mimosa pudica, folds her leaves when touched. Cells at the base of each leaf lose water quickly and go soft, and the leaf drops.
examples: A limp coriander bunch stands up again after an hour in water.
A plant that is not watered droops because her cells are losing water.
Celery left in strong salt water goes bendy, and celery in plain water stays crisp.
explanations.art: A balloon filling with water inside a shoebox and pushing the sides tight, beside a stem cross-section with full round cells and a wilted one with shrunken cells.

explanations.concept: Why cells are small: surface and inside
explanations.definition: A cell takes in food and oxygen and lets out waste through her surface. As a cell grows bigger, her inside grows faster than her surface, so a large cell would have too little surface for her size.
explanations.description: Take a cube that is 1 centimetre on each side. Its surface is 6 square centimetres and its inside is 1 cubic centimetre. Double the cube to 2 centimetres on each side. The surface becomes 24 square centimetres, which is 4 times more. But the inside becomes 8 cubic centimetres, which is 8 times more. The inside grows faster than the surface. A cell needs food and oxygen to get to every part of her inside, and they all arrive through the surface. So a cell that grows too big starves in the middle. Most cells are between 10 and 100 micrometres wide. A few get very large by finding other ways. A hen's egg yolk is one huge cell, but it is mostly stored food and is not busy inside. Some nerve cells are very long, but they are thin like threads.
examples: A crushed piece of ice melts much faster than a whole cube, because it has far more surface.
A flat leaf cell is thin, so no part is far from the surface.
A nerve cell in your leg can be more than a metre long, but it is thinner than a hair.
explanations.art: A 1 cm cube and a 2 cm cube side by side, with their surfaces coloured and the number of small cubes inside shown: 1 cube and 8 cubes.

explanations.definition: A single-celled living thing is a whole being made of one cell. That one cell takes in food, makes energy, senses her surroundings, moves, gets rid of waste and divides to make more.
explanations.description: Your body has different cells for different jobs. A single cell has to do every job herself. An amoeba pushes out a part of herself and flows forward. When she meets food, she wraps herself round it, and the food ends up in a bubble inside her where it is broken down. A paramecium swims by beating thousands of tiny hairs. She can back away from an obstacle and try another way. Pond water keeps flowing into her by osmosis, so she has a small pump called a contractile vacuole that pushes the extra water out again and again. A euglena has chloroplasts and makes sugar in the light, and she can also swim towards the light with a whip-like tail and sense it with a red spot. A bacterium senses food and swims towards the smell. A single cell is not a half-made body. She is a complete life.
examples: An amoeba wraps round a smaller cell and takes it in.
A paramecium swims backwards when she bumps into something.
A yeast cell in dough takes in sugar and makes carbon dioxide gas.
explanations.art: Three single cells in a drop of water: an amoeba wrapping round a green cell, a slipper-shaped paramecium covered with hairs, and a green euglena with a tail.

explanations.concept: Mitochondria and chloroplasts: visitors who stayed
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria that were taken inside larger cells more than a billion years ago and stayed as partners. This is called endosymbiosis.
explanations.description: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small loops of DNA, their own double membranes, and they divide on their own inside the cell, like bacteria do. Their DNA is more like the DNA of bacteria than that of the cell they live in. Lynn Margulis, an American biologist, argued for this in 1967, and her paper was turned down by many journals before one published it. At first, many biologists thought the idea was wild. Since then, DNA studies have shown that she was right. A mitochondrion cannot live outside her cell now, and the cell cannot live without her mitochondria. So your cells are built out of partnerships. Scientists still argue about exactly how the first partnership began.
examples: The mitochondria in your cells have their own DNA, which you inherit only from your mother.
The chloroplasts of a leaf are descended from bacteria that could already catch sunlight.
Some sea slugs take chloroplasts from the algae they eat and keep them working inside their own cells for weeks.
explanations.art: A large cell swallowing a small bacterium, then the same bacterium living inside as a bean-shaped mitochondrion with its own small loop of DNA.

explanations.concept: How the first cell began: skin, instructions or chemistry first?
explanations.definition: Nobody knows how the first cell began. Scientists agree on two things: it happened more than 3.5 billion years ago, and the first cells were much simpler than any cell alive today.
explanations.description: A cell needs three things at once: a skin to hold her together, instructions that can be copied, and chemistry that releases energy. Each of them seems to need the others. Scientists have different ideas about which came first, and none of the ideas is proven. We do know that fatty molecules put in water make little bubbles on their own, so a skin is not hard to get. We also know that RNA, a cousin of DNA, can both carry instructions and speed up some chemical reactions. Scientists have also found chemical reactions that run on their own on the rocks near hot underwater vents.
examples: Fat molecules shaken in water form hollow bubbles, a little like cell skins.
Some RNA molecules can copy parts of themselves.
Hot vents on the sea floor, such as the Lost City field in the Atlantic Ocean, release chemicals that can power simple reactions.
explanations.art: Three small panels: a hollow fat bubble in water, a strand of RNA copying itself, and a hot underwater vent with chemicals streaming from rock.

perspectives.explanation: A bubble of fat in water could hold chemicals together long enough for them to react. Once there was a bubble, chemicals inside could slowly become more complex.
RNA can store a message and also act as a tool. A first molecule that could copy herself could start evolution, and a skin could come later.
Reactions on rock near hot vents could have made the building blocks and the energy first. Skins and instructions might have grown out of that.

agreed.text: Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and DNA.
agreed.evidence: Every kind of cell that has been studied, from bacteria to human nerve cells, has been found to have all three.

agreed.text: The cell membrane is made of two layers of fatty molecules with proteins set into it.
agreed.evidence: In 1925 Evelyn Gorter and François Grendel measured the fat from red blood cells and found twice as much as one layer needs. Electron microscopes later showed the two layers directly.

agreed.text: Water passes through a membrane towards the side with more dissolved stuff, and this is called osmosis.
agreed.evidence: Wilhelm Pfeffer measured it in 1877 using a man-made membrane. Every test since, such as potato strips in salt water, has agreed.

agreed.text: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Animal cells do not.
agreed.evidence: Microscopes show these parts clearly in plant cells such as onion, Hydrilla and leaf cells, and they are absent from animal cells such as cheek cells.

agreed.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria.
agreed.evidence: They have their own loops of DNA that look like bacterial DNA, and they divide on their own inside the cell.

agreed.text: Single-celled living things are fully alive and can sense, move, eat and divide.
agreed.evidence: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw them swimming in pond water in the 1670s. Later biologists watched them feed and divide.

challenging.claim: The nucleus is the brain or the boss of the cell.
challenging.who: Many textbook pictures and popular comparisons.
challenging.for: The nucleus holds the DNA, which carries the instructions for building the cell. Without the nucleus, most cells cannot make new proteins for long.
challenging.against: Bacteria have no nucleus and run perfectly well. A human red blood cell lives about four months with no nucleus. The cytoplasm does most of the work, and the nucleus is more like a library than a boss.

challenging.claim: Every living thing is either a plant or an animal.
challenging.who: Carl Linnaeus and the biology books that followed him in the 1700s.
challenging.for: Most large living things we see are clearly plants or clearly animals.
challenging.against: A euglena has chloroplasts like a plant and swims like an animal. Mushrooms are neither. Bacteria are a separate and very different kind of cell. Biologists now sort living things into several large groups.

challenging.claim: A single-celled living thing is simple.
challenging.for: A single cell is very small and has far fewer parts than a body.
challenging.against: A single cell does every job a body does, with no organs to help her. A paramecium backs away from obstacles and a bacterium senses food and steers towards the smell. A single cell holds thousands of different molecules, all working together.

challenging.claim: A body is a team of separate cells working together.
challenging.who: Some biologists who describe a body as a community of cells.
challenging.for: Cells can be grown on their own in a lab. Many cells in a body have their own life cycle and die or divide.
challenging.against: Cells in a body signal each other all the time and cannot live alone for long without the right surroundings. Others say it makes more sense to call the body one living being whose cells are its parts.

challenging.claim: The cell membrane is a fixed, solid wall.
challenging.who: Early drawings of cells and some old textbooks.
challenging.for: The membrane keeps the cell together and keeps things in and out.
challenging.against: S. Jonathan Singer and Garth Nicolson proposed in 1972 that the membrane is fluid, with fat molecules and proteins that slide around, like icebergs in a sea. Later experiments confirmed it.

big_questions.q: A potato strip went floppy in salt water, and it never touched anything except her skin. If water goes through a cell's skin in both directions, what decides which way it goes?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you found in the cups. What was different on the two sides of the skin?

big_questions.q: A cell's skin must let food in and keep her own chemicals from leaking out. How can one skin do both jobs?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Gatekeeper game, where the gatekeeper treats different visitors differently.

big_questions.q: Bacteria have no nucleus, and they still pass on instructions to their children. Where could the instructions be kept?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a cell has inside her skin.

big_questions.q: Why are there no cells as big as a mango?
big_questions.hint: Think about the ice race and the cubes. What happens to the surface when something gets bigger?

big_questions.q: Is a cell a thing, or is she something that keeps happening? What if the skin stopped choosing for one minute?
big_questions.hint: A stone stays a stone while nothing happens to it. Does a cell stay a cell?

big_questions.q: You are about 30 trillion cells, and each one is alive. Are you one living being, or a crowd of living beings that live together?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cells in your gut, skin and blood. Which of them could live on their own, and for how long?

big_questions.q: An amoeba has no brain, yet she finds food and moves away from danger. What would you have to see an amoeba do to say that she thinks?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you decide that your friend, or a crow, is thinking.

big_questions.q: If life began on another planet, would the first cells there also need a skin? Why or why not?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a skin does for the chemistry inside it.

story.title: The Thirsty Seedlings
story.note: A made-up story. Pokkali rice, which grows in the salty backwater fields near Kochi in Kerala, is real, and so is the way salt draws water out of cells. The people, the amounts of salt and the seedling test are imagined. Scientists who study Pokkali are still working out exactly how the plant copes with salt, so the story only gives the part they agree on.
text: In Kumbalangi, near Kochi, the backwater comes into the paddy fields twice a day. At high tide, the water is salty. At low tide, it flows back out.

Anjana was in Class 4. She lived with her mother and her grandmother, Ammamma. Every year, Ammamma sowed a rice called Pokkali in the flooded fields. She kept the seed in a clay pot in the kitchen, as her own mother had done.
'Other rice dies in this water,' said Ammamma. 'Pokkali grows in it.'
Anjana's friend Rafi lived next door. His father sold rice in the market, and Rafi thought he knew about rice. 'Water is water,' he said. 'A plant drinks it. Why would a bit of salt matter?'
'Let's find out,' said Anjana.

On Saturday, she filled two steel tumblers with tap water. In one she stirred half a spoon of salt. She tasted a drop, and it was as salty as the backwater in the dry months. Rafi's father had given them two seedlings of ordinary paddy, the same age and the same size. They stood one seedling in each tumbler, in the same window.
'Now we wait,' said Anjana.
By evening, the seedling in plain water stood straight. The seedling in the salty water was drooping. Her leaves were rolled up tight, like a person hugging themselves.
Rafi stared. 'But she is standing in water,' he said. 'How can she be thirsty? That makes no sense.'
Anjana did not know. She sat on the kitchen step, with her chin in her hands, and watched the seedling droop.
Behind her, Ammamma was making mango pickle. She had cut green mangoes into small pieces and mixed in a big handful of salt. 'Leave it overnight,' she said, and she covered the bowl with a plate.

Next morning, Anjana lifted the plate. At the bottom of the bowl was a pool of water. The mango pieces were smaller and softer. Nobody had squeezed them. Nobody had added water. And the water was not in a tumbler. It came out of the mango.
Anjana stood very still.
'Ammamma,' she said, 'the salt pulled the water out of the mango.'
'Of course,' said Ammamma. 'That is how pickle keeps. Everyone knows that.'
'But the mango was not in water,' said Anjana. 'The salt was outside. The water was inside. And it came out.' She ran to the window and looked at the drooping seedling.

Beena Teacher had told the class something last week, and Anjana had not thought it mattered. Every cell has a thin skin. The skin lets water through, in both directions. And water goes towards the side with more dissolved stuff.

'It's the same thing,' Anjana said. 'The roots are made of tiny cells. Each cell is like a little piece of mango. The salt is outside them, so their water goes out to the salty side. The seedling is standing in water and her cells are losing water to it. She is thirsty because the water is too salty.'
Rafi had come over to see. 'That's strange,' he said. 'So the salt pulls the water out of the plant.'
'Salty water does. Plain water does not,' said Anjana. 'Look at the other seedling.'
They looked at the one in plain water. Her leaves were fresh and green. Her stem was firm. Her cells were full.
'So how does Pokkali do it?' asked Rafi.
Ammamma laughed. 'Ask the rice.'
That afternoon, they went to the field with Ammamma. A Pokkali plant stood in the brown water, tall and green. Anjana touched a leaf. It was as firm as the seedling in plain water.

'Beena Teacher says scientists have studied this rice for years,' said Anjana. 'They have found that the plant keeps most of the salt out of her roots. The little salt that gets in, she packs away in her oldest leaves, where it does less harm. But scientists are still finding out how she does it.'
'She has been doing it for hundreds of years,' said Ammamma. 'Long before anyone knew about cells.'
Rafi looked at the plant for a long time. 'So she is not just drinking,' he said. 'She is working all the time to stay full of water.'
'Yes,' said Anjana. 'Everyone's cells do that.'

That evening, Anjana put the ordinary seedling from the salty tumbler into plain water. She did not know whether the seedling would recover. By the next morning, a little of the green had come back. Two days later, the leaves were standing up again.

Anjana wrote in her notebook: 'A plant can be thirsty while standing in water. If the water is salty, the water goes out of her cells and into the salty water.' Then she drew a small mango piece, a seedling and a line of tiny cells, with arrows going out.
story.epiphany: A plant can be thirsty while standing in water, because salty water pulls the water out of her cells.

games.title: Cell Detectives: who am I?
games.context: This is a clue game. Each card gives a clue about a part of a cell, or a kind of cell. You say who it is, then turn the card over to check.
rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and make a pile with the clue side up.
The reader takes the top card and reads the clue aloud. The reader does not turn it over.
Everyone else has ten seconds to say the answer out loud. For a card with a question, say the answer and the reason.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. A player who was right keeps the card. If nobody was right, the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
Take turns being the reader. The first player to keep 6 cards wins.
Playing alone: go through the pile once and keep the cards you got right. Then play again and try to keep more.

setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the clue. Everyone has ten seconds to answer.

printables.title: 24 two-sided clue cards: a clue on the front and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: I am the thin skin around every cell. I decide what comes in and what goes out. Who am I?
items.b: The cell membrane. I am made of two layers of fat molecules with proteins set into me.

items.f: I am the jelly that fills a cell. Most of the cell's work happens in me. Who am I?
items.b: The cytoplasm. I am mostly water, and the parts of the cell float in me.

items.f: I keep the instructions for building and running the cell, written in DNA. In many cells I am a round room. Who am I?
items.b: The nucleus. I keep the DNA safe, like a library.

items.f: I am a stiff box outside the membrane. Plant cells have me and animal cells do not. Who am I?
items.b: The cell wall. I give a plant cell her box shape and help her stand up.

items.f: I am green. I catch sunlight and use it to make sugar. Who am I?
items.b: The chloroplast. My green colour is what makes a leaf green.

items.f: I am a bag of water. In a plant cell I am huge and push against the wall to keep the cell firm. Who am I?
items.b: The vacuole. When I am full, the cell is firm. When I lose water, the plant wilts.

items.f: I release energy from food. A hard-working muscle cell has thousands of me. Who am I?
items.b: The mitochondrion. Plant cells have me too, and I have my own little loop of DNA.

items.f: A cell has a wall, many chloroplasts and one big vacuole. Is she a plant cell or an animal cell?
items.b: A plant cell. The wall, the chloroplasts and the big vacuole are the three things plant cells have and animal cells do not.

items.f: A cell has no wall and no chloroplasts, and she can be round, flat or long. Plant cell or animal cell?
items.b: An animal cell. With no stiff wall, animal cells can be many shapes.

items.f: A bacterium has no nucleus. Where is her DNA?
items.b: In the cytoplasm, in a loop. Bacteria have DNA, but the DNA floats loose instead of sitting in a nucleus.

items.f: A potato cell is put in strong salt water. Does water move into the cell or out of the cell?
items.b: Out of the cell. Water moves through the membrane towards the side with more dissolved stuff, so the cell goes soft.

items.f: A limp coriander leaf stands up again after an hour in water. Which part of each cell is pushing on the wall?
items.b: The big vacuole. It fills with water and pushes on the cell wall, and the cell goes firm again.

items.f: A mature human red blood cell lives for about four months. What does she not have?
items.b: A nucleus. She loses it as she grows up, and carries oxygen around the body without one.

items.f: Which single-celled living being flows into any shape and wraps herself round her food?
items.b: The amoeba. She pushes out a part of herself and closes it round the food.

items.f: Which single-celled living being swims with thousands of tiny hairs and pumps extra water out of herself?
items.b: The paramecium. She uses a small pump called a contractile vacuole to push out the water that keeps flowing in.

items.f: Which single-celled living being has green chloroplasts and a whip-like tail?
items.b: The euglena. She makes sugar in the light, and can also swim towards the light.

items.f: What were mitochondria and chloroplasts before they lived inside cells?
items.b: Free-living bacteria. They moved into larger cells long ago and stayed as partners.

items.f: A mushroom cell has a wall but no chloroplasts. Is a mushroom a plant or an animal?
items.b: Neither. Fungi are a group of their own, with cell walls like plants but no chloroplasts.

items.f: Why can a cell not grow as big as a mango?
items.b: Her inside grows faster than her surface. Food and oxygen come in through the surface, so they would not reach the middle.

items.f: Name four things that both plant cells and animal cells have.
items.b: A membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus and mitochondria.

items.f: Oxygen is tiny. How does it cross the cell membrane?
items.b: It slips straight between the fat molecules of the membrane, with no help.

items.f: Sugar is too big to slip through the membrane. How does it get into a cell?
items.b: Through carrier proteins in the membrane, which pass it across.

items.f: A grain of starch is far too big to enter a cell. What does the body do first?
items.b: It cuts the starch into sugar in digestion. Sugar can then be carried in.

items.f: A cell uses energy to push salt out through her membrane. What part of the membrane does this?
items.b: A pump. Pumps are proteins in the membrane, and they use energy to push things across against the way they would go.

flow.say: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Put them in a pile with the clue side up. Who will be the first reader?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Make a pile.

flow.do: Play the first rounds. The reader reads the clue aloud and does not turn the card. Everyone answers. The reader turns the card and reads the back aloud. Whoever was right keeps the card.
flow.say: Read the clue aloud. Wait for the answers. Then turn the card and read the back. Whoever was right keeps the card.
flow.kid: Read a clue. Answer. Turn the card. Did you get it right?

ask.q: Which part of a cell would you most like to be, and why?
good: The nucleus, because it holds the instructions.
The membrane, because it decides what passes.
Any answer with a reason is good.

flow.parent: Read the reason on the back each time, even when the answer was right. The reasons are the learning. If nobody gets a card, put it at the bottom.

check.q: A cell has a wall, chloroplasts and a big vacuole. Which kind of cell is she?
options: A plant cell
An animal cell
A bacterium
check.why: Those three parts belong to plant cells. Animal cells have no wall and no chloroplasts, and a bacterium has no nucleus or big vacuole. If you picked animal, check the plant-only list again.

games.title: Gatekeeper: who gets through the skin?
games.context: This is a sorting game about the cell membrane. You are the gatekeeper in the skin of a cell. Each visitor card names something that wants to cross the skin, and you decide what happens to it.
rules: Cut out the 13 visitor cards and the 4 gate signs: PASS, HELPER, PUMP and BLOCK. Cut out the 5 energy tokens. Put the tokens in the middle.

PASS means the visitor slips through the skin with no help. HELPER means a carrier protein passes the visitor across. PUMP means the cell uses 1 energy to push the visitor across. BLOCK means the visitor cannot get through.

One player is the gatekeeper. The reader reads the front of a visitor card. The gatekeeper puts one gate sign face down. With 3 or 4 players, the others may whisper advice to the gatekeeper, but only the gatekeeper places the sign.
The reader turns the card over. If the sign matches the back, the cell scores a point. If the sign was wrong, the cell loses 1 energy token. A correct PUMP also costs 1 energy token.
If the energy tokens run out, the cell has stopped working and the game ends. If all 13 cards are played with energy left, the cell wins.
Take turns being the gatekeeper after every four cards. Playing alone: you are the gatekeeper for every card.

setup.caption: 2. The gatekeeper puts a gate sign face down for each visitor.
