printables.title: 13 two-sided visitor cards: the visitor on the front and what the skin does on the back

items.f: Oxygen, a tiny molecule with no charge, outside a muscle cell.
items.b: PASS. Oxygen slips between the fat molecules of the membrane with no help.

items.f: Carbon dioxide, a tiny molecule with no charge, leaving a cell.
items.b: PASS. Like oxygen, it slips straight through the fat layer.

items.f: Water, around a potato cell sitting in plain water.
items.b: PASS. Water crosses the membrane in both directions, a little by itself and faster through water channels. It ends up on the side with more dissolved stuff.

items.f: A vitamin that dissolves in fat, such as vitamin A.
items.b: PASS. It dissolves in the fat of the membrane, so it slides through. Ernest Overton noticed this in the 1890s.

items.f: Alcohol, made by a yeast cell.
items.b: PASS. The molecules are small, so the alcohol leaves the yeast cell through the membrane.

items.f: Glucose, a sugar, outside a muscle cell.
items.b: HELPER. Glucose is too big and too watery to slip through, so a carrier protein in the membrane passes it across.

items.f: Amino acids, the building blocks for proteins, outside a cell.
items.b: HELPER. Special carrier proteins in the membrane take amino acids across.

items.f: Sodium from salt has leaked into a nerve cell. The cell needs it out again.
items.b: PUMP. A pump protein uses energy to push sodium out, against the way it would naturally go.

items.f: Potassium that the cell needs to gather inside, where there is already plenty.
items.b: PUMP. The same pump that pushes sodium out brings potassium in. It uses energy.

items.f: Calcium, which the cell keeps very low inside.
items.b: PUMP. Pumps push calcium out of the cell, and each push costs energy.

items.f: A grain of starch from a roti.
items.b: BLOCK. Starch is far too big. Digestion first cuts it into sugar, and sugar can then be carried in.

items.f: A big protein from food, such as one from dal.
items.b: BLOCK. Whole proteins are too big. Digestion cuts them into amino acids first.

items.f: A germ, which is a whole bacterium, next to a skin cell.
items.b: BLOCK. A whole bacterium is far too big to cross a cell's membrane. Your body has other defences too.

flow.do: Cut out the cards, the signs and the tokens. Put the energy tokens in the middle. Read the four signs aloud and say what each one means.
flow.say: Cut out everything. PASS means no help. HELPER means a carrier protein. PUMP costs energy. BLOCK means it cannot get through.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Learn the four signs: PASS, HELPER, PUMP, BLOCK.
flow.parent: If you are playing alone, put the visitor cards in a pile and play the gatekeeper for every card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gatekeeper. You get the game ready and learn the four signs.

flow.do: The reader reads a visitor card. The gatekeeper puts a sign face down. The reader turns the card over and reads the back. Score a point for a match. Take away 1 energy for a wrong sign or a correct PUMP.
flow.say: Read the visitor. The gatekeeper picks a sign and puts it face down. Turn the card over and read the back aloud.
flow.kid: Read the visitor. Pick a sign. Turn the card. Were you right?

ask.q: Which visitors were the easiest to sort, and why?
good: The ones that are tiny, like oxygen.
The ones that are very big, like starch.

flow.parent: Read the reason on the back each time. If the cell runs out of energy, talk about why: real cells run out of energy too, and pumps stop when they do. Then play again.
flow.context: In this step you play the game. The back of each card says why.

flow.do: Count the points and the energy tokens left. Ask your child what the skin does that a wall does not.
flow.say: Count the points. Count the energy tokens left. What can the skin do that a plain wall cannot do?
flow.kid: Count your points. What can the skin do that a wall cannot?
flow.think: Why does the skin need energy to pump, when it needs none to let oxygen through?

check.q: Which visitor needs the cell to spend energy to get across?
options: Sodium that must be pushed out
Oxygen going in
Carbon dioxide leaving
check.why: A pump uses energy to push something across against the way it would naturally go. Oxygen and carbon dioxide slip straight through the fat layer, so they need none. If you picked oxygen, look at the PASS cards again.

flow.context: This is the last step of Gatekeeper. You count the points and think about what a skin does.

worksheets.title: Parts of a cell and what water does

items.p: Which part of a cell decides what goes in and what comes out?
opts: The cell membrane
The cytoplasm
The nucleus
items.why: The membrane is the thin skin around the cell. It lets some things pass, helps some across and blocks the rest. The cytoplasm is the jelly inside, and the nucleus keeps the DNA.

items.p: Where does a bacterium keep her DNA?
opts: Inside a round nucleus
Floating loose in the cytoplasm
Inside the cell membrane
items.why: Bacteria have no nucleus. Their DNA is a loop that floats in the cytoplasm. Plant, animal and fungus cells keep their DNA in a nucleus.

items.p: Animal cells have a stiff cell wall outside the membrane.
items.why: False. Plant cells, fungus cells and bacteria have a cell wall. Animal cells do not, which is why animal cells can be many shapes.

items.p: The green part of a plant cell that catches sunlight is the ____.
items.why: Chloroplasts hold the green colour that catches sunlight and uses it to make sugar. Animal cells have none.

items.p: Match each cell part to its job.
pairs: Membrane
decides what passes in and out
Cytoplasm
the jelly where most of the cell's work happens
Nucleus
keeps the DNA that holds the instructions
Vacuole
a bag of water that keeps a plant cell firm
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part has its own job. The membrane is the skin, the cytoplasm is the working jelly, the nucleus is the instruction room, and a big vacuole pushes on the wall of a plant cell.

items.p: A potato strip goes floppy in strong salt water. What happened to the water that was inside its cells?
opts: Some of it moved out into the salty water
More of it moved in from the salty water
It turned into salt
items.why: Strong salt water has more dissolved stuff than the inside of the cells. Water moves through the cell skin towards the saltier side, so the cells lose water and the strip goes soft.

items.p: Sort each cell part by where it is found.
items.a: as given
items.why: Plant cells have three extra parts: a wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Everything else on this list is found in both kinds of cell.

items.p: Salt can pull water out of mango pieces even though the pieces are not sitting in any water.
items.why: True. The salt sits on the outside of the cells, and water moves out through the cell skins towards it. That is why a pool of water collects at the bottom of a bowl of salted mango.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 4 in Madurai, finds that her strip in cup A droops 2 mm after 40 minutes, and her strip in cup C droops 26 mm. How many times more does the strip in C droop than the strip in A?
items.why: 26 divided by 2 is 13. The strip in strong salt water drooped 13 times as much, because the salt was the only thing that was different.

items.p: A friend says: 'A plant cannot be thirsty when she is standing in water.' What would you tell your friend?
items.a: A plant can be thirsty in salty water. Salt outside the root cells pulls water out of them, so the cells lose water and the plant wilts, even though water is all around. In plain water, the cells stay full.
items.why: A strong answer says that salty water pulls water out of the cells, and mentions osmosis or the cell skin. It may use the potato strip or the pickle as evidence.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Amoeba, paramecium, euglena, mushroom.
items.a: The mushroom, because a mushroom is made of many cells. The other three are each a single cell.
items.why: An amoeba, a paramecium and a euglena are whole living beings made of one cell. A mushroom is a fungus made of many cells.

items.p: Draw a plant cell. Label the wall, the membrane, the nucleus, a chloroplast and the big vacuole.
items.a: A box-shaped cell with a thick wall outside a thin membrane, a round nucleus, several small green ovals and one large vacuole filling most of the space.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the wall outside the membrane, and the vacuole pushing against the wall. It does not show a round cell with no wall.

items.p: Why does a limp coriander bunch stand up again when you put the stems in water?
opts: The leaf cells fill with water and push against their walls
The leaf cells grow new walls
The leaf cells turn green again
items.why: Cells that have lost water are soft. When water comes back, the vacuoles fill and push on the walls, and the cells and leaf go firm.

items.p: Water that moves through a skin towards the side with more dissolved stuff is called ____.
items.why: Osmosis is the movement of water through a membrane towards the side with more dissolved stuff such as salt or sugar.

items.p: Put these in order to say what happens to a potato strip left in strong salt water.
a: There is more dissolved salt outside the potato cells than inside
Water moves out through the skin of each cell
The cells lose water and lose their firmness
items.why: The salt outside is what starts it. Water follows through the cell skins, the cells go soft, and then the whole strip bends.

items.p: A classmate says: 'The nucleus is the boss of the cell and tells everything what to do.' What is a better way to describe the nucleus?
items.a: The nucleus is like a library. It keeps the DNA safe, and the cell copies out the pages she needs. A bacterium has no nucleus and still works well, and a red blood cell lives for months without one.
items.why: A strong answer says the nucleus keeps the instructions, and does not order everything around. Bacteria and red blood cells show that a cell can work without a nucleus.

items.p: Oxygen crosses the cell membrane with no help, but sugar needs a carrier protein. What is the best reason?
opts: Oxygen is tiny and slips between the fat molecules, but sugar is too big and watery
Oxygen is heavier than sugar
Sugar is alive and oxygen is not
items.why: The membrane is made of fat. Tiny molecules with no charge, like oxygen, slip between the fat molecules. Sugar is bigger and mixes with water, so it needs a helper protein.

items.p: Which part of the membrane uses energy to push salt out against the way it would go?
opts: A pump protein
A water channel
A layer of fat
items.why: A pump is a protein in the membrane that spends energy to push things across. Water channels and fat layers need no energy.

items.p: Water can only move into a cell through the membrane. It can never move out.
items.why: False. Water moves through the membrane in both directions. Which way more of it goes depends on where there is more dissolved stuff.

items.p: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living ____ that moved into larger cells.
items.why: Both have their own loops of DNA that look like bacterial DNA, and they divide on their own. Lynn Margulis argued for this in 1967 and it was later confirmed.

items.p: Match each single-celled living being to what she does.
pairs: Amoeba
flows into any shape and wraps round her food
Paramecium
swims with tiny hairs and pumps out extra water
Euglena
has chloroplasts and a tail, and swims towards light
Yeast
makes a new cell by growing a bud
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these is a whole being made of one cell, and each does the jobs of life in her own way.

items.p: A cube is 3 cm on each side. A cube has 6 faces. How many square centimetres is the whole outside surface of the cube?
items.why: Each face is 3 times 3, which is 9 square centimetres. Six faces make 6 times 9, which is 54 square centimetres.

items.p: Explain why a cell as big as a mango could not stay alive, using the idea of surface.
items.a: A cell takes in food and oxygen through her surface. When a cell gets bigger, her inside grows much faster than her surface, so the surface cannot supply the middle. The middle would starve.
items.why: A strong answer says that things enter through the surface and that the inside grows faster than the surface. It may use the cube or the ice race as evidence.

items.p: Sort each feature by which cell has it.
items: a loop of DNA floating loose
items.a: as given
items.why: A bacterium has no nucleus and no chloroplasts, and her DNA is loose in the cytoplasm. Both kinds of cell have a membrane, a wall and cytoplasm.

items.p: Why can mango pickle stay good for months in a jar?
opts: Salt pulls water out of the microbes' cells, so they cannot grow
Salt makes the microbes eat faster
Salt turns the mango into oil
items.why: Microbes are cells too. Salt outside them pulls water out of their cells, so they dry up and cannot grow. Oil and a closed jar help too.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Salt drawing water out of brinjal slices. A pool of water at the bottom of salted mango. A raisin swelling in water. Water drying from a wet cloth.
items.a: Water drying from a wet cloth. The others are water moving through cell skins towards the side with more dissolved stuff.
items.why: Drying cloth is evaporation, where water leaves into the air. The other three are osmosis, where water moves through the skins of cells.

items.p: A euglena has chloroplasts and makes sugar in the light, and she also swims and can eat. Three scientists disagree about what she is.

views.says: She has chloroplasts and makes her own food, so she is a kind of plant.
She swims, senses light and can eat, so she is a kind of animal.
She is neither. Single-celled living things with a nucleus form a very large group of their own.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use something you know about the euglena. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses evidence, for example: the modern biologist, because the euglena does what both plants and animals do, so the two boxes are too small. It may say that the plant scientist is right about the chloroplasts.
items.why: There is no single right answer to pick. A strong answer gives a reason from what the euglena does, and says what another view gets right.

items.p: Draw an amoeba eating a smaller cell. Show the food and how the amoeba takes it in.
items.a: A blob-shaped cell with two arms pushed out, curling round a small cell, and a bubble forming round the food inside her.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the amoeba wrapping around the food and the food ending up in a bubble inside her cytoplasm.

items.p: Evelyn Gorter and François Grendel spread the fat from red blood cells on water. It covered about twice the surface of the cells. What did they conclude?
opts: The skin of a cell is two layers of fat thick
The cells were twice as big as they looked
The cells had no skin
items.why: If the fat could cover twice the surface of the cells, then the skin must have been two layers thick. Their numbers were rough, but electron microscopes later showed two layers.

items.p: Why did scientists in the 1870s say that a living cell skin must exist, even though nobody could see it?
opts: Water and dissolved stuff moved in and out as though through a skin
They had photographed it
A book said so
items.why: Wilhelm Pfeffer and others saw that water moved in a way only a thin skin could explain. When a tool cannot see something, scientists can still tell it is there from what it does.

items.p: A paramecium lives in pond water, which has far less dissolved stuff than her insides. Using osmosis, explain why water keeps flowing into her, and what her pump does.
items.a: Her cytoplasm has more dissolved stuff than the pond water, so water moves into her through her membrane all the time. Her pump, the contractile vacuole, collects the extra water and pushes it out, so she does not swell and burst.
items.why: A strong answer says water moves towards the side with more dissolved stuff, which is inside her, and that the pump pushes the extra out.

items.p: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus.
items.why: True. Red blood cells lose their nucleus as they mature. They carry oxygen for about four months without one.

worksheets.title: Salt, skins and the first cells

items.p: After a cyclone, seawater floods a rice field. The rice plants wilt, even though they are standing in water. Explain why, using what you know about cells.
items.a: The seawater has a lot of dissolved salt, so the water inside the root cells moves out into it through the cell skins. The cells lose water, and the plant wilts, even though she stands in water.
items.why: A strong answer says that salty water outside the root cells pulls water out of them by osmosis. It may mention that a salt-tolerant rice such as Pokkali keeps most salt out of her roots.

items.p: A raisin is 12 mm long. After a night in plain water, it is one and a half times as long. How long is it now?
items.why: One and a half times 12 is 12 plus 6, which is 18. The raisin is 18 mm long, because its cells took in water.

items.p: A hospital drip is made with a little salt, about 9 grams in a litre of water, and not with plain water. Why?
opts: Plain water would make blood cells swell and burst, and the salt keeps the balance
Salt makes the drip taste nicer
Salt kills germs in the drip
items.why: Blood cells sit in a liquid with some dissolved stuff in it. In plain water, water would move into them and swell them. A drip with about the same amount of salt as blood keeps them the right size.

items.p: A red blood cell put in plain water would swell, and one put in strong salt water would shrink.
items.why: True. In plain water, water moves into the cell. In strong salt water, water moves out. Red blood cells have no wall, so they cannot hold their shape against the swelling.

items.p: Oral rehydration solution is water with a little salt and sugar. It helps a person who has lost water from diarrhoea. Using what you know about carriers and osmosis, suggest why it helps.
items.a: The cells lining the gut have carrier proteins that take in sugar and salt together. When sugar and salt move into the cells, water follows by osmosis. So the sugar and salt help water get in.
items.why: A strong answer says carriers bring sugar and salt into the gut cells together, and water follows. Plain water alone is taken in more slowly. The solution was first used widely in 1971 by Dilip Mahalanabis.

items.p: You have about 30 trillion cells, and each cell is alive. Three people disagree about what you are.

views.says: You are a crowd of living cells that cannot live apart for long. The body is a community.
You are one living being. Your cells depend on each other so much that it makes no sense to treat them as separate.
You are both. How many beings there are depends on how you choose to count.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Use something you know about cells. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses evidence, for example: the doctor, because red blood cells and nerve cells cannot live alone. It may say that the cell biologist is right that each cell is alive.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives a reason from what cells do, and says what another view gets right.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found about cell skins.
pairs: Wilhelm Pfeffer
measured how water moves through a man-made skin, in 1877
Ernest Overton
noticed that substances that dissolve in fat get into cells fastest
Evelyn Gorter and François Grendel
showed that the cell skin is two layers thick, in 1925
Singer and Nicolson
said that the skin is a fluid with proteins floating in it, in 1972
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each step added a clue. First came the idea that a skin exists, then that it is fatty, then that it has two layers, and then that it flows.

items.p: Fat molecules have a head that likes water and a tail that avoids water. In water, why do they form a double layer with the tails inside?
opts: The tails hide from the water between the two layers of heads
The heads push the tails together
Fat molecules always stack in twos
items.why: The heads face the water on both sides and the tails tuck away from it in the middle. This happens on its own, which is one reason scientists think skins formed early.

items.p: Put these steps in the order that scientists found them out.
a: Pfeffer showed that water moves as though through a skin (1877)
Overton showed that fat-soluble substances get in fastest (1890s)
Gorter and Grendel showed the skin is two layers thick (1925)
Singer and Nicolson said the skin flows like a fluid (1972)
items.why: Each result built on the one before. First the skin was needed to explain how water moved, then it was found to be fatty, then to be two layers, and then to flow.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Yeast, a bacterium, a euglena, a red blood cell in your body.
items.a: The red blood cell in your body. The others each live as a whole being on their own.
items.why: Yeast, a bacterium and a euglena are whole living beings, each made of one cell. A red blood cell in your body depends on the rest of your body to stay alive.

items.p: Draw two potato cells side by side, one in plain water and one in strong salt water. Draw arrows to show which way the water moves.
items.a: A full, round cell in plain water with arrows pointing in, and a shrunken cell in salt water with arrows pointing out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the cell in plain water swollen with arrows into it, and the cell in salt water shrunken with arrows out of it.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out if sugar water pulls water out of potato strips as well as salt water does. Say what you change and what you keep the same.
items.a: I change the dissolved stuff: one cup of sugar water and one of salt water. I keep the same: strips cut from one potato, the same amount of water, the same amount of sugar and salt, and the same time. I also use a cup of plain water as a control.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, keeps the rest the same, and includes a plain water cup to compare with.

items.p: Which of these about the first cell is still debated?
opts: Whether the skin, the instructions or the chemistry came first
Whether the first cells lived more than three billion years ago
Whether fat molecules can form hollow bubbles in water
items.why: Scientists agree that the first cells appeared more than 3.5 billion years ago, and that fat bubbles form easily. What came first is still open.

items.p: A plant stands up because the water in the big vacuole pushes against the cell ____.
items.why: The wall is stiff, so the water pressure from inside makes the whole cell firm. When the water is lost, the pressure drops and the plant wilts.

items.p: Scientists know for certain how the very first cell began.
items.why: False. Nobody knows. Scientists have several ideas and none is proven.

projects.title: Hay Pond: a week of looking for single-celled swimmers

materials.item: 1 clean glass jar, about 500 millilitres
a pinch of dry grass, hay or a few dry leaves
300 millilitres of water, boiled by a grown-up and then cooled
1 teaspoon of water from a flower vase, a pot plant saucer, a puddle or a pond
a phone camera or a magnifier, and a torch
a plate or lid to cover the jar loosely, and a notebook
a second small jar for a comparison (optional)

projects.safety: A grown-up boils the water. Do not drink or taste the pond water. Wash your hands after touching the jar. Keep the jar covered so mosquitoes cannot lay eggs in it, and throw the water down a drain at the end.
projects.record: Draw the jar on days 1, 3, 5 and 7. Write how cloudy the water is, what it smells like, and what you see in the torch beam.
projects.context: In this project you grow a small pond in a jar and look for single-celled living things over a week. You may see only cloudy water and tiny moving specks. A microscope would be needed to see their shapes.

schedule.what: Pour the cooled water in the jar, add the grass and a teaspoon of pond or vase water. Cover loosely. Put it near a window, out of direct sun.
Look at the water in a torch beam. Is it cloudy? Does it smell? Draw the jar.
Shine the torch through the side. Look for tiny specks that move. Use a magnifier or a phone camera.
Look one last time. Draw what you see. Say who lives in your pond, and what they might be eating.

setup.art: A glass jar with a pinch of dry grass in cooled water, a teaspoon of pond water being added, and a plate covering the jar loosely.
setup.caption: 1. Put grass and cooled water in a jar. Add a teaspoon of pond or vase water. Cover loosely.

setup.art: The jar on a windowsill, with the water getting cloudy and a torch shining through the side.
setup.caption: 2. Keep the jar by a window. Shine a torch through the side every two days.

setup.art: A child holding a phone camera close to the jar, looking at tiny white specks moving in the beam.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5 and day 7, look for tiny moving specks with a magnifier or phone camera.

flow.do: A grown-up boils the water and lets it cool. Pour 300 millilitres into the jar. Add the pinch of grass and 1 teaspoon of pond or vase water. Cover the jar loosely and put it near a window. Ask your child what might grow in the jar.
flow.say: Pour the cooled water into the jar. Add the grass and a teaspoon of pond or vase water. Cover it loosely. Put it by a window.
flow.kid: Make the pond. Water, grass, a teaspoon of pond water. Cover it loosely.

ask.q: What do you think might grow in the jar? Why?
good: Tiny living things from the pond water.
Nothing, because the water was boiled.

flow.parent: If you have no pond or puddle, use a teaspoon of water from a flower vase or the saucer of a pot plant. Single-celled living things often arrive on the grass itself as resting cells. Do not use a tight lid, because the microbes need air. A few grains of uncooked rice also work in place of grass. For a fair comparison, set up a second jar with grass but no pond or vase water, and see which one turns cloudy. With 2-4 children, each child can start a jar with water from a different place (vase, puddle, plant saucer) and compare; one child alone can use one jar.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hay Pond. You start the pond.

flow.do: On day 3, look at the water. Is it cloudy? Does it smell? Shine the torch through the side of the jar in a dark room. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Shine the torch through the side. Is the water cloudy? Does it smell? Draw the jar.
flow.kid: Shine a torch through the jar. Is it cloudy? Draw what you see.
flow.parent: By day 3 the water is usually cloudy, and may smell a little like a pond. That is normal. The cloudiness is mostly bacteria. Larger swimmers, if any, usually come in the next few days.
flow.context: In this step you look at the pond on day 3. Cloudy water means that bacteria are growing.

flow.do: On day 5, shine the torch through the side. Look slowly for tiny white specks that move. Use a magnifier or a phone camera close to the glass. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Look for tiny specks that move. Use the torch and the magnifier. Look slowly. Draw what you see.
flow.kid: Look for tiny moving specks. Use the torch. Look slowly.

ask.q: What do you see that moves? What might it be doing?
good: Maybe they are looking for food.

flow.parent: Larger single cells such as paramecia are about two tenths of a millimetre long, so you may see them as moving white specks in a torch beam. You will not see their shape without a microscope. If you see nothing, wait up to five more days; hay jars often take 5 to 10 days. A phone camera held against the glass, with the torch behind the jar, helps most. Many jars show only cloudiness, and that is still a good result. A clip-on phone microscope or a Foldscope would show more.
flow.context: In this step you look for single-celled swimmers. They may be too small to see well.

flow.do: On day 7, look one last time. Compare your four drawings. Ask your child who lives in the pond, and what they might be eating. Then throw the water away and wash the jar.
flow.say: Compare your four drawings. Who lives in your pond? What might they be eating? What do they need?
flow.kid: Compare your drawings. Who lives in your pond? What do they eat?
flow.think: Nobody put these living beings in the jar on purpose. Where did they come from?

check.q: The boiled water in the jar was clear on day 1 and cloudy on day 3. What does the cloudiness show?
options: Living things from the pond water and the grass have been growing
The grass has dissolved
The water has got old
check.why: Boiling kills the microbes. The pond water and the grass brought new ones, and they eat and divide, so the water turns cloudy. If you picked dissolved grass, check whether the grass changed.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Hay Pond. You compare your drawings and think about who lives there.

experiments.title: Potato Strips: what does salt water do to a cell?
experiments.question: What happens to potato strips left in plain water, a little salt water and a lot of salt water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 40 minutes, which strip will be the stiffest and which will be the floppiest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the strips come from one potato and are cut to the same size. Each cup holds the same amount of water, 200 millilitres, and the strips stay in for the same time. Only the salt changes. Cup A has no salt and is the control. Cup B has a little. Cup C has a lot. Any difference between the strips comes from the salt.

materials.item: 1 firm potato with no green patches and no sprouts
3 steel tumblers or cups, about 250 millilitres each
600 millilitres of water at room temperature
5 level teaspoons of table salt
a knife, used only by a grown-up
a ruler marked in millimetres
a marker pen and 3 paper labels
tissue paper or a clean cloth, a timer and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the potato with the knife. Do not eat the strips afterwards. Wash your hands when you finish.
experiments.record: Write the sag in millimetres for each strip at the start, at 20 minutes and at 40 minutes, and what each strip feels like. Then draw a line graph with one line for each cup.
experiments.context: In this experiment you find out what salt water does to the cells of a potato. You change one thing only, the salt, and measure how stiff the strips become.

setup.art: A potato being cut into six equal strips, each about one centimetre wide and six centimetres long, on a chopping board.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts six strips of the same size from one potato.

setup.art: Three tumblers labelled A, B and C, with plain water, a little salt being stirred in, and a lot of salt being stirred in.
setup.caption: 2. Fill three cups with 200 millilitres of water. A gets no salt, B gets 1 teaspoon, C gets 4 teaspoons.

setup.art: A child pinching a potato strip by one end and holding a ruler beside the free end to read how far it hangs down.
setup.caption: 3. Pinch each strip near one end. Measure how far the tip droops, then put two strips in each cup.

setup.art: A timer showing 20 minutes beside the three cups, and a child taking a strip out and patting it dry with a cloth.
setup.caption: 4. After 20 minutes and again after 40, take a strip out, pat it dry and measure the droop.

flow.do: Show the three cups. Say what goes in each. Ask your child to guess which strip will be stiffest and which will be floppiest, and to say why. Write down both.
flow.say: We will put potato strips in three cups. Cup A has plain water. Cup B has a little salt. Cup C has a lot of salt. After 40 minutes, which strip will be stiffest? Which will be floppiest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three cups. A is plain. B has a little salt. C has a lot. Which strip ends up floppiest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that strip will be the floppiest?
good: Salt takes something out of the potato.
I think the salt will change the water inside.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the results table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Potato Strips test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts six strips from one potato, each 1 centimetre wide and 6 centimetres long. Cut them thin, about 5 millimetres. Put 200 millilitres of water in each cup. Stir 1 teaspoon of salt into B and 4 teaspoons into C. Stir C for a full minute. Label the cups.
flow.say: Pour 200 millilitres of water into each cup. Stir one level teaspoon of salt into B. Stir four teaspoons into C. Stir C until you cannot see any salt. Write A, B and C on the labels.
flow.kid: Pour water into three cups. Stir 1 spoon of salt into B. Stir 4 spoons into C.
flow.parent: Cut the strips about the same size, because thick strips stay stiff longer. Any cups that hold 200 millilitres will do, not only steel ones. With 2-4 children, give each child one cup to look after and measure, with one child as timer and one as recorder. One child alone does all three cups. Four teaspoons dissolve in 200 millilitres if you stir for a minute. Leave cup A with no salt, because it is the control.

check.q: Why does cup A get no salt?
options: So we can compare the other strips with a strip that had no salt
Because strips do not like salt
To save salt
check.why: Cup A is the control. It differs from the other cups in one way only, the salt, so any change in B or C comes from the salt.

flow.context: In this step you set up the three cups. Each cup gets a different amount of salt.

flow.do: Pinch one strip about 1 centimetre from its end and hold it flat, with the rest sticking out sideways. Hold a ruler upright by the free tip. Read how far the tip hangs down in millimetres. Do this for all six strips. Write the numbers. Put two strips in each cup. Start the timer.
flow.say: Pinch a strip near one end and hold it flat. Read how far the tip droops, in millimetres. Do all six strips. Then put two strips in each cup and start the timer.
flow.kid: Pinch a strip. Measure how far the tip droops. Then put two in each cup.
flow.parent: A fresh potato strip hardly droops at all, so the numbers at the start are typically 0 to 3 millimetres. Measure the same way every time, with the same length of strip sticking out.

check.q: Why do we measure the strips before they go in the cups?
options: So we know how stiff each strip was at the start
To make the strips wet
So the strips know the way
check.why: Without a starting number, a change cannot be measured. The start is what each later reading is compared with.

flow.context: In this step you measure how stiff each strip is before the test, and then start the test.

flow.do: At 20 minutes, take one strip from each cup. Pat it dry. Measure the droop the same way. Write the number and what the strip feels like. Put it back. Repeat at 40 minutes. While you wait, read the cell membrane card.
flow.say: At 20 minutes, take one strip from each cup and pat it dry. Measure how far the tip droops, and feel it. Write both down. Do it again at 40 minutes.
flow.kid: Take a strip out. Pat it dry. Measure the droop. Feel it. Write it down.

ask.q: What do you notice about the strips in cup C?

flow.parent: Typically the strip in A stays stiff, B droops a little, and C droops a lot and feels rubbery by 40 minutes. If all three are still stiff, check that the salt in C really dissolved, and leave the strips for an hour more. A strip in plain water may feel even firmer than at the start. That is also a result.

check.q: After 40 minutes the strip in cup C droops much more than the strip in cup A. What does this show?
options: Water left the potato cells and went into the salty water
Water went into the potato cells from the salty water
The salt got inside the cells and made them hard
check.why: Cups A and C differ only in the salt. Strong salt water pulls water out through the skin of the cells. The cells lose their firmness and the strip goes floppy. If you picked the second one, check which strip was floppy, and which was firm.

flow.context: In this step you measure and feel the strips twice. The numbers show what the water did to the cells.

flow.do: Draw a line graph with minutes along the bottom and droop up the side. Draw one line for each cup. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each cup. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the strip in strong salt water went floppy because the salt was outside, and that water left the cells. After they have said what they saw, explain: water passes through the thin skin of every cell in both directions, and ends up on the side with more dissolved stuff. This is osmosis. Plain water gives a firm strip, because the cells have more dissolved stuff inside than outside, so water moves in.
flow.think: A potato strip in plain water for a whole night might even grow a little longer and firmer. Why might that happen?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Potato Strips test. You draw the graph and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Naked Egg: a skin you can see and measure
experiments.question: What happens to an egg with no shell when it sits in plain water, and then in thick syrup?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will the egg look and feel like with no shell? Will it get bigger or smaller in plain water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: One egg is measured around its middle at every stage with the same piece of string. Between measurements it stays in the same kind of jar at room temperature. Only the liquid changes, first plain water and then thick syrup, so any change in size comes from the liquid.
results_table: What it looks and feels like

materials.item: 1 raw hen's egg, not cracked (buy 2, in case one skin tears)
1 tall glass jar or a wide steel tumbler
about 2 cups of white vinegar
a piece of string about 30 centimetres long and a ruler
about 1 cup of honey (one small bottle), or thick sugar syrup made from 1 cup of sugar dissolved in half a cup of hot water and cooled
a bowl, a spoon and a kitchen towel

experiments.safety: Handle the raw egg gently over a bowl, because it breaks easily. Do not eat the egg or taste the liquids. Wash your hands after touching the egg. If your family does not handle raw egg, skip this and do the Potato Strips and Raisin Swell tests instead. Raw egg can carry germs, so wash hands and the bowl with soap after touching it.
experiments.record: Write the distance around the egg on days 3, 4 and 5, and what it looks and feels like. Draw the egg at each stage.
experiments.context: In this experiment you dissolve the shell of a raw egg and watch the thin skin that is left. The skin lets water through like the skin of a cell, so the egg swells or shrinks.

schedule.what: Guess. Put the egg in a jar and cover it with vinegar. Watch the bubbles.
Gently pour off the vinegar and add fresh vinegar.
Rinse the egg. Measure around it. Put it in plain water.
Measure again. Move the egg into honey or syrup.
Measure a last time. Say what happened and why.

setup.art: A raw egg lying in a glass jar completely covered with vinegar, with tiny bubbles on the shell.
setup.caption: 1. Put the egg in a jar and cover it with vinegar. Bubbles rise from the shell.

setup.art: A child gently pouring the old cloudy vinegar into a bowl and pouring in fresh vinegar, the shell partly gone.
setup.caption: 2. On day 2, pour off the old vinegar and add fresh vinegar.

setup.art: A child holding a shell-less egg under a tap with both hands, the egg pale and slightly see-through, and a string around its middle.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, rinse the egg and measure around its middle with string.

setup.art: The same egg in plain water, then in honey, with a string measure beside each jar and the egg a different size.
setup.caption: 4. Put the egg in plain water, then in honey. Measure it each day.

flow.do: Show your child the egg. Ask what will happen to the shell in vinegar, and what the egg will be like with no shell. Then put the egg in the jar. Cover it with vinegar. Watch the bubbles.
flow.say: We will put an egg in vinegar for two days. What do you think will happen to the shell? What will the egg be like without a shell? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: An egg goes into vinegar for two days. What happens to the shell? Why?

ask.q: What can you see on the shell in the vinegar?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The vinegar is an acid, and the shell is made of calcium carbonate. They react and make carbon dioxide, which is the gas in the bubbles. Cover the jar loosely and keep it out of the sun. If your kitchen is very hot, keep the jar in the fridge, and then the shell may take 3 days. With 2-4 children, give each pair its own egg and jar, so everyone can measure, or share one egg with children taking turns to measure.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Naked Egg test. You guess, and then you set up the jar.

flow.do: On day 2, gently pour off the old vinegar into a bowl without tipping the egg. Add fresh vinegar. Look at the egg. The shell should be mostly gone.
flow.say: Pour off the old vinegar slowly, and keep the egg in the jar. Add fresh vinegar. What has happened to the shell?
flow.kid: Pour off the old vinegar. Add new vinegar. How does the egg look now?
flow.parent: After one to two days the shell is usually all gone, and there is a cloudy scum on top. If a few bits of shell are left on day 3, leave the egg in vinegar for one more day.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Naked Egg test. You change the vinegar so the shell keeps dissolving.

flow.do: On day 3, lift the egg out with a spoon over a bowl. Rinse it gently under cool water. Rub any left-over bits of shell off very gently with your thumbs under the tap. Wrap string around the middle and measure it. Write the number. Put the egg in a jar of plain water.
flow.say: Rinse the egg gently. Hold it in two hands, over a bowl. Wrap string round the middle and measure it. Then put the egg in plain water.
flow.kid: Rinse the egg gently. Measure around the middle. Put it in plain water.

ask.q: What does the egg look and feel like without its shell?

flow.parent: The egg is covered by a thin, tough skin that holds it together, and you can see the yellow yolk through it. It breaks if dropped or squeezed. The skin is called the shell membrane. It is not the same as the cell membrane around the yolk, but it lets water through in the same way. A hen's egg yolk is one huge cell.

check.q: Why do we measure around the egg with the same string every time?
options: So the numbers can be compared fairly
Because string is waterproof
So the egg stays still
check.why: The same method each time means any change in the numbers comes from the egg, not from measuring in a different way.

flow.context: In this step you measure the egg with no shell and put it into plain water.

flow.do: On day 4, lift the egg out and measure around the middle. Write the number. Put the egg in a jar and pour honey or thick syrup over it until it is covered. The egg will float, so turn it over every few hours, or press a small plate on top.
flow.say: Measure around the egg again. What is different? Then move the egg into the honey or syrup jar.
flow.kid: Measure the egg again. Is it bigger? Put it in honey.

ask.q: Did the egg get bigger, smaller or stay the same? Why do you think so?

flow.parent: After a day in water, the egg is typically about 0.5 to 1.5 centimetres bigger around, so use a soft string and read it to the nearest half centimetre. It may look pale and clear. If you see no change, the egg may have a tiny crack. Try a new egg.
flow.context: In this step you measure the egg after a day in plain water, then move it into thick syrup.

flow.do: On day 5, lift the egg out gently and measure around the middle. Look at the skin. Write the number. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Measure the egg for the last time. Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Measure the egg. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: After one day the egg in honey is typically smaller and wrinkled, and honey works better than thin syrup, because water left the egg and went into the thick sugar syrup. After they have said what they saw, explain: water crosses the thin skin in both directions and ends up on the side with more dissolved stuff. In plain water the egg swelled. In syrup it shrank. Wash hands, then throw the egg and the liquids away.
flow.think: A hen's egg is one huge cell. What else in the kitchen is a single cell?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Naked Egg test. You say what happened and why.

activities.title: Limp to Crisp: bring a wilted herb back to life

materials.item: 1 bunch of coriander, mint or spinach, bought the day before
2 tumblers
200 millilitres of plain water and 200 millilitres of strong salt water, made with 2 level teaspoons of salt
a knife used by a grown-up, a marker pen and 2 paper labels

schedule.what: Leave the bunch out on the counter, away from the fridge and the sun, until the next day.
Cut the stem ends, stand half the bunch in plain water and half in salt water, and check after 15 and 30 minutes.

activities.record: Draw the two bunches at the start and after 30 minutes. Measure with a ruler how high the tallest sprig stands above the cup rim at the start, at 30 minutes and at 60 minutes. Write which bunch stood up.
activities.context: In this activity you bring a wilted herb back to life with water, and see what salt water does instead. It shows why a plant stands up when her cells are full.

setup.art: A bunch of coriander lying limp on a kitchen counter next to a clock showing the next morning.
setup.caption: 1. Leave the bunch on the counter overnight until it goes limp.

setup.art: Half a bunch standing in a tumbler of plain water and half standing in a tumbler of salt water, both labelled.
setup.caption: 2. Cut the stem ends. Stand half in plain water and half in salt water.

setup.art: The same two tumblers after 30 minutes: the plain-water bunch standing up and the salt-water bunch still drooping.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, look at both bunches.

flow.do: Leave the bunch on the counter overnight, out of the fridge and out of the sun. Ask your child to guess how it will look tomorrow, and what will bring it back.
flow.say: Leave this bunch out overnight. How do you think it will look tomorrow? What might make it stand up again? Why?
flow.kid: Leave the bunch out. Guess how it will look tomorrow. Why?
flow.parent: In a warm kitchen, coriander goes limp in a few hours. If your bunch is still firm, leave it for longer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Limp to Crisp. You let the herb go limp, and you guess.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts 1 centimetre off the end of every stem. Split the bunch in two. Stand one half in plain water and one half in salt water. Look at both after 15, 30 and 60 minutes. Measure how high the tallest sprig stands above the rim each time. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Cut the stem ends. Put half the bunch in plain water and half in salt water. Look after 15 minutes and again after 30.
flow.kid: Cut the stems. Put half in plain water, half in salt water. Look after 30 minutes.

ask.q: What is different between the two bunches?

flow.parent: Typically the plain-water bunch stands up within 30 to 90 minutes and the salt-water bunch stays limp or gets floppier. Cold water works faster, and so does letting the leaves sit in the water too. With 2-4 children, make four small bunches and let each child watch one, or split into plain and salt teams. Water climbs up the cut stem and moves into the leaf cells. In salt water the cells cannot fill. If neither bunch changes, leave both for two hours. After they have said what they saw, explain: leaf cells are firm when their big vacuoles are full of water. Salty water outside pulls water out of the cells, and plain water lets them fill.
flow.think: Why do shopkeepers sprinkle water on vegetables, but not salt water?

check.q: A limp herb stands up again in plain water. What has changed inside the leaf?
options: The cells have filled with water and gone firm
The cells have grown new walls
The cells have turned green
check.why: A limp leaf has cells that have lost water. When water comes back, the vacuoles fill and push on the cell walls, and the leaf stands up. If you picked new walls, notice how quickly it happened, in only half an hour.

flow.context: In this step you set up the two tumblers and watch the herbs. One tumbler has plain water and one has salt water.

activities.title: Ice Race: why more surface means faster change

materials.item: 2 ice cubes of the same size from one tray
2 steel katoris or small plates of the same size
a clean cloth and a rolling pin
a timer

activities.safety: A grown-up crushes the ice. Keep the ice away from the face.
activities.record: Write how many minutes the whole ice cube and the crushed ice take to melt completely.
activities.context: In this activity you race a whole ice cube against the same amount of crushed ice. It shows why a cell needs a lot of surface for her size.

setup.art: Two ice cubes on a counter, and a clean cloth wrapped round one of them with a rolling pin lying beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap one ice cube in a cloth. A grown-up crushes it with a rolling pin.

setup.art: A whole ice cube in one katori and a heap of crushed ice from the other cube in a second katori, side by side.
setup.caption: 2. Put the whole cube in one katori and the crushed ice in the other.

setup.art: The two katoris after ten minutes: the crushed ice already melted to water and the whole cube just starting to shrink.
setup.caption: 3. Check every 5 minutes. Which one melts first?

flow.do: Show the two cubes. Ask your child which will melt first: a whole cube or the same amount crushed. Ask for a reason. Write down both.
flow.say: Here are two cubes of ice. One will stay whole. One will be crushed into tiny pieces. Which will melt first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One ice cube stays whole. One is crushed. Which melts first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will melt first?
good: More of the ice touches the air.
There is more outside to get warm.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ice Race. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up wraps one cube in a cloth and crushes it with a rolling pin into small pieces. Put the whole cube in one katori and all the crushed ice in the other. Put both on the counter. Start the timer.
flow.say: Wrap one cube in a cloth. A grown-up crushes it. Put the whole cube in one katori and the crushed ice in the other. Start the timer.
flow.kid: Crush one cube in a cloth. Put each in a katori. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Use cubes from the same tray, so they weigh the same. Keep both katoris in the same spot, away from the fan.
flow.context: In this step you crush one cube and start the race.

flow.do: Check both katoris every 5 minutes. Write how much ice is left in each. Note the time when each one is fully melted. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Look every five minutes. When did the crushed ice finish melting? When did the whole cube finish? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Look every five minutes. Which melts first? Why?
flow.parent: The times depend on how warm your kitchen is. Typically the crushed ice melts about two to four times faster than the whole cube. A whole cube may take 15 to 40 minutes, and the crushed ice 5 to 15. With 2-4 children, give one child each job: timer, whole-cube watcher, crushed-ice watcher and recorder. One child alone can do all four. After they have said what they saw, explain: heat only reaches the ice through its surface. The crushed pieces have much more surface in all, so heat reaches all of the ice faster. A cell takes in food and oxygen through her surface in the same way, which is why cells stay small.
flow.think: If a cell grew as big as a mango, how would food reach the middle?

check.q: Why does crushed ice melt faster than a whole cube of the same amount?
options: It has more surface for the warmth to reach
It is colder to start with
It has less water in it
check.why: Warmth gets into the ice through its surface. The same amount of ice, crushed into small pieces, has far more surface. If you picked colder, both came from the same tray.

flow.context: In this step you watch the race and say why one won.

activities.title: Build a Plant Cell and an Animal Cell from the kitchen

materials.item: 1 rectangular box, such as a tiffin box or a shoebox lid with cardboard sides, for the plant cell wall
1 zip bag or a katori covered with cling film, for the animal cell membrane
1 cup of thick curd or besan paste for the cytoplasm of each cell
1 ball of atta dough the size of a lemon, split in two, for the two nuclei
a handful of green moong beans or green peas for chloroplasts
a few rajma or black beans for mitochondria
1 small zip bag filled with water for the big vacuole of the plant cell
toothpicks and paper flags for labels
1 thin plastic sheet or bag to line the box

activities.record: Draw both cells and label the parts. Write the three parts that only the plant cell has.
activities.context: In this activity you build a plant cell and an animal cell out of kitchen things. You see which parts they share, and which parts only a plant cell has.

setup.art: A tiffin box with a thin plastic sheet inside, filled with curd, with green peas, a dough ball and a water-filled bag inside.
setup.caption: 1. Plant cell: box for the wall, curd for the cytoplasm, a dough ball for the nucleus, green peas for chloroplasts, a water bag for the vacuole.

setup.art: A zip bag lying flat and filled with curd, a dough ball and a few beans, with no box round it.
setup.caption: 2. Animal cell: a zip bag for the membrane, with curd, a dough ball and beans.

setup.art: Paper flags on toothpicks labelling each part of both models.
setup.caption: 3. Label every part with a paper flag.

flow.do: Lay out all the things. Ask your child which thing could stand for each cell part. Name the skin, the jelly, the instruction room, the green parts, the water bag and the stiff box. Let them choose first.
flow.say: Here are the kitchen things. Which one could be the jelly? Which could be the nucleus? Which could be the stiff wall? Choose first.
flow.kid: Look at the things. Which could be the jelly? The nucleus? The wall?

ask.q: Which part of the cell is the stiff box?
good: The wall that only plants have.

flow.parent: There is no single right choice. Suggest the kitchen things only if they are stuck.
flow.context: This is the first step of the cell models. You choose which thing stands for which part.

flow.do: Build the animal cell first. Spoon curd into a zip bag. Add a dough ball for the nucleus and a few rajma beans for mitochondria. Seal the bag. Then build the plant cell. Put a thin plastic sheet in the box, then curd, a dough ball, peas, beans and the water bag. Press the water bag against one side.
flow.say: Build the animal cell in a zip bag with curd, a dough ball and beans. Build the plant cell in a box. Add peas and a water bag.
flow.kid: Build the animal cell in a bag. Build the plant cell in a box.
flow.parent: Wash hands before and after, and throw the food away afterwards. With 2-4 children, each child or pair builds one cell and then compares. One child alone builds both. Use a katori with cling film if you have no zip bag. The water bag is the big vacuole of the plant cell. In the animal cell you could add a very small water bag for a small vacuole.

check.q: Which parts does the plant cell model have that the animal cell model does not?
options: The box, the green peas and the big water bag
The curd, the dough ball and the beans
The zip bag and the curd
check.why: A plant cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a big vacuole. Animal cells have the membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria, as plant cells do, but no wall or chloroplasts.

flow.context: In this step you build both cells. The animal cell has a bag for a skin. The plant cell also has a box for a wall.

flow.do: Add a paper flag to each part. Look at both models. Ask your child what is the same, what is different, and what the plant cell can do that the animal cell cannot. Then close your eyes while a grown-up hides one part, and name the missing part.
flow.say: Label every part. What is the same in both cells? What is different? What can the plant cell do that the animal cell cannot?
flow.kid: Label every part. What is the same? What is different?

ask.q: What can the plant cell do that the animal cell cannot?

flow.think: A mushroom cell has a wall but no chloroplasts. How would you change the plant cell model to make a mushroom cell?
flow.context: In this step you label your models and compare the two cells.

activities.safety: Check for allergies to milk, wheat, chickpea and beans before you start. Do not eat any of it, because raw rajma beans make people ill. Keep beans and toothpicks away from small children, who may put them in their mouths.

activities.title: Raisin Swell: plain water or salt water?

materials.item: 12 raisins of the same kind
2 small cups or steel katoris
100 millilitres of plain water and 100 millilitres of strong salt water, made with 2 level teaspoons of salt
a marker pen and 2 paper labels, and a ruler

activities.record: Draw a raisin from each cup, and write how big each one looks and feels the next morning.
activities.context: In this activity you leave raisins in plain water and in salt water overnight. Raisins are dried grapes, so you can see what water does to dried-up cells.

schedule.what: Put 6 raisins in each cup. Guess what each cup will do. Leave overnight.
Look at, measure and feel the raisins. Say why they changed.

setup.art: Six wrinkly raisins in a cup of plain water and six in a cup of salty water, both cups labelled.
setup.caption: 1. Put 6 raisins in each cup, one with plain water and one with strong salt water.

setup.art: The same two cups the next morning: plump smooth raisins in the plain water and still wrinkly raisins in the salt water.
setup.caption: 2. Next morning, look at, measure and feel the raisins.

flow.do: Measure the longest side of 3 raisins from the packet and write the average. Put 6 raisins in each cup. Pour plain water in one and strong salt water in the other. Ask your child to guess what each cup of raisins will look like tomorrow, and why.
flow.say: Put six raisins in each cup. One cup has plain water. One has strong salt water. What will each look like tomorrow? Why?
flow.kid: Six raisins in each cup. Plain water in one. Salt water in the other. Guess why.

ask.q: Which raisins do you think will change the most? Why?
good: The ones in plain water, because they are dry.

flow.parent: Use the same raisins and the same amount of water in each cup. Soak for 8 to 12 hours. With 2-4 children, each child can have their own two cups.
flow.context: This is the first step of Raisin Swell. You set up the two cups and guess.

flow.do: Next morning, take out 3 raisins from each cup. Look at them, measure the longest side of each, write the average and squeeze them gently. Draw both. Ask your child what they saw and why.
flow.say: Take one raisin out of each cup. Look, measure and squeeze. Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Take a raisin out of each cup. Look. Squeeze. What changed?
flow.parent: Raisins in plain water are typically plump and smooth, often clearly bigger than at the start. Raisins in salt water stay smaller and more wrinkly, although they may swell a little. After they have said what they saw, explain: a raisin is a dried grape, packed with sugar. Plain water has less dissolved stuff than the raisin's cells, so water moves in. Strong salt water has nearly as much, so less water moves in.
flow.think: Why do we put raisins in warm milk or water before making payasam?

check.q: Why did the raisins in plain water swell?
options: Water moved into their sugary cells
The raisins grew new cells overnight
Air filled the raisins
check.why: A raisin's cells hold a lot of dissolved sugar. Plain water has less, so water moves in through the skins of the cells. The cells swell. Growing new cells would take far longer.

flow.context: In this step you compare the raisins. You say what the water did.

activities.safety: Do not eat the soaked raisins. Wash your hands afterwards.

videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check it is accurate before adding it.

quiz.p: Which three things do almost all cells have?
opts: A membrane, cytoplasm and DNA
A wall, a leaf and a root
A nucleus, a brain and a heart
quiz.why: Every cell has a membrane for a skin, cytoplasm for her working jelly, and DNA for her instructions. Bacteria have no nucleus, and not every cell has a wall.

quiz.p: What is the main job of the cell membrane?
opts: To decide what goes in and out of the cell
To make sugar from sunlight
To store the DNA
quiz.why: The membrane is the skin of the cell. It lets some things pass, helps some across, and stops the rest. Making sugar is the job of chloroplasts and storing DNA is the job of the nucleus.

quiz.p: Which of these is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
opts: Chloroplasts
A nucleus
Cytoplasm
quiz.why: Plant cells have a wall, chloroplasts and a big vacuole as well. Plant and animal cells share the nucleus and cytoplasm.

quiz.p: A potato strip stays stiff in plain water but goes soft in salt water. What is the best explanation?
opts: Water leaves the cells of the strip and goes into the salty water
The salt makes the potato rot quickly
The potato drinks the salt and gets heavy
quiz.why: Strong salt water has more dissolved stuff than the potato cells have. Water moves through the cell skins towards the saltier side, so the cells go soft. Rot would take days.

quiz.p: Which sentence about water and a cell's skin is correct?
opts: Water moves through the skin in both directions and ends up on the side with more dissolved stuff
Water can only enter a cell and can never leave
Water cannot pass through a cell's skin at all
quiz.why: Water crosses the membrane both ways all the time. More ends up on the side that has more dissolved stuff. This is osmosis.

quiz.p: Why can a cell not grow as big as a mango?
opts: Her inside grows faster than her surface, so the middle would not get food and oxygen
Her membrane would be too thin to see
Her nucleus would get too hot
quiz.why: Food and oxygen come in through the surface. When a cell gets bigger, her inside grows faster than her surface, so the middle would starve.

quiz.p: Which single-celled living being has chloroplasts and swims with a tail?
opts: Euglena
Amoeba
Yeast
quiz.why: A euglena makes sugar in the light like a plant and swims towards the light like an animal. An amoeba flows along without a tail, and yeast does not swim.

quiz.p: How does a paramecium get rid of the extra water that flows into her?
opts: A small pump called a contractile vacuole pushes it out
She drinks it
Her wall squeezes it out
quiz.why: Pond water has less dissolved stuff than her insides, so water keeps flowing in. Her contractile vacuole collects it and pumps it out again and again.

opts: The cell's DNA, which carries the instructions
The cell's sugar
The cell's water
quiz.why: The nucleus is the room that keeps the DNA safe. The cell copies out the pages of instructions she needs.

quiz.p: Which of these has no nucleus?
opts: A bacterium
A cheek cell
A mushroom cell
quiz.why: Bacteria keep their DNA loose in the cytoplasm. Animal, plant and fungus cells keep their DNA in a nucleus.

quiz.p: What were mitochondria before they lived inside larger cells?
opts: Free-living bacteria
Tiny plants
Pieces of the nucleus
quiz.why: Mitochondria have their own loops of DNA and divide on their own. They began as bacteria that moved into larger cells and stayed.

quiz.p: How do we know a cell has a skin, even though early microscopes could not see it?
opts: Water and dissolved stuff moved in and out as though through a skin, and fat tests showed it was there
A scientist guessed it and nobody checked
Because a plant cell has a wall
quiz.why: Scientists such as Wilhelm Pfeffer and Ernest Overton inferred a fatty skin from how water and other substances moved. Electron microscopes later showed it.

quiz.p: Why does a plate of cut brinjal slices get wet after you sprinkle salt on it?
opts: Salt pulls water out of the cells of the brinjal
The salt melts the brinjal
The salt makes water out of air
quiz.why: Salt on the outside of the cells makes water move out through the cell skins. The water collects on the plate.

quiz.p: The cell wall of a plant cell is the same thing as her cell membrane.
quiz.why: False. The wall is a stiff layer outside the membrane. The membrane is a thin, fatty skin that decides what passes in and out.

applications: Pickling mango, lime and vegetables with salt, which pulls water out of the microbes' cells so they cannot grow.
Making jam and keeping honey, where a lot of sugar stops microbes growing in the same way.
Hospital drips made with a little salt, so that blood cells do not swell or shrink.
Oral rehydration solution for diarrhoea, first used widely in 1971 in refugee camps by Dilip Mahalanabis and his team, where carriers take sugar and salt in and water follows.
Growing salt-tolerant rice such as Pokkali in the salty backwater fields of Kerala.
Medicines such as penicillin, which stop bacteria from building their cell walls. Human cells have no wall, so they are not harmed.
Watering plants and keeping vegetables fresh by sprinkling them with water.
Salting cucumber or brinjal slices before cooking, to draw out water.
Choosing how much salt to put on a plant bed or in a pot, because too much will make the plants wilt.
Using microscopes to see cells in blood tests, which doctors use to find illness.

open_questions.q: How did the very first cell begin: with a skin, with instructions, or with chemistry?
open_questions.why_open: The first cells lived more than 3.5 billion years ago and left almost no traces. Scientists have several ideas and cannot test them against the real thing.

open_questions.q: What is the smallest cell that can stay alive and make copies of herself?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016, scientists built a bacterium with only 473 genes. They still did not know what about a third of those genes do.

open_questions.q: How did a cell get a nucleus?
open_questions.why_open: Cells with a nucleus came from cells without one, but scientists argue about how. Some think a bacterium moved into an archaeon, and others think the nucleus formed from the cell's own membranes.

open_questions.q: Do single cells have feelings, or do they only react?
open_questions.why_open: We can see an amoeba choose and a bacterium steer. What it is like to be one cannot be measured, so scientists disagree about what to call it.

open_questions.q: How many different kinds of single-celled living things are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have named only a small share of them, and most have never been grown in a lab.

open_questions.q: Could life on another planet be made of cells?
open_questions.why_open: All life we know is cells, so we have nothing to compare with. Scientists think any life would need some kind of boundary, but nobody has found any.

ask_kids: What do you think is happening to the water in your tumbler when you put salt in?
If you were a cell, what would you let through your skin, and what would you keep out?
Where in the kitchen do you see water moving out of food when salt is added?
Why is a cucumber crisp but a day-old one is soft?
Which of your body's cells do you think is the biggest? Which is the longest?
If a single cell can eat, move and sense, what do you think she does when she is scared?
Why do you think plants are green but mushrooms are not?
What would a cell look like in a world with no water?

jokes.j: What did the animal cell say to the plant cell?
jokes.a: 'You are so stiff!' The plant cell said, 'It is called a cell wall, thank you.'

jokes.j: What do cells like to snack on?
Why did the potato strip go to the doctor?
jokes.a: It was feeling a bit limp after a swim in salt water.

jokes.j: What kind of music do cells like?
Why did the paramecium bring a bucket to the pond?
jokes.a: To get rid of all the water she kept pumping out.

jokes.j: What did the nucleus say to the cytoplasm?
jokes.a: 'I will keep the recipes safe. You do the cooking.'

jokes.j: Why was the membrane such a good gatekeeper?
jokes.a: It never let the wrong molecules pass, and it always checked their passes.

jokes.j: Why did the amoeba never get lost?
jokes.a: She could change direction, and shape, whenever she liked.

jokes.j: Why was the chloroplast always in a good mood?
jokes.a: It spent all day in the sun.

maths.problem: In the Potato Strips test, the strip in cup C drooped 3 mm at the start, 11 mm at 20 minutes and 24 mm at 40 minutes. If it keeps drooping by the same amount in the next 20 minutes as it did in the last 20, how much will it droop at 60 minutes?
maths.explain: From 20 to 40 minutes it drooped 24 minus 11, which is 13 mm more. Adding 13 mm to 24 mm gives 37 mm. This is a guess from the line on the graph, because the strip cannot droop for ever.
maths.context: In the Potato Strips test you measure how far a strip droops at three times and draw a line graph.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows how fast something changes, and lets you make a sensible guess about what comes next.

maths.problem: In the Ice Race, the whole cube took 24 minutes to melt and the same amount of crushed ice took 8 minutes. How many times faster did the crushed ice melt? What does that tell you about its surface?
maths.explain: 24 divided by 8 is 3. The crushed ice melted 3 times as fast, because it had much more surface for the warmth to reach.
maths.context: In the Ice Race you time a whole ice cube against the same amount of crushed ice.
maths.why_maths: A ratio compares two numbers by how many times bigger one is. It turns two times into one clear idea about surface.

maths.problem: A cube of jaggery is 1 cm on each side. Its surface is 6 square centimetres and its inside is 1 cubic centimetre. A bigger cube is 4 cm on each side. Find its surface, its inside and the surface for every cubic centimetre inside. Which cube has more surface for its size?
maths.answer: The big cube has a surface of 96 square centimetres and an inside of 64 cubic centimetres. That is 1.5 square centimetres of surface for each cubic centimetre. The small cube has 6.
maths.explain: Each face of the big cube is 4 times 4, which is 16 square centimetres. Six faces make 96. The inside is 4 times 4 times 4, which is 64. Then 96 divided by 64 is 1.5. The small cube has 6 divided by 1, which is 6. The small cube has far more surface for its size, and that is why cells stay small.
maths.context: This problem follows the Ice Race and the idea that a cell takes in food through her surface.
maths.why_maths: Surface is an area and the inside is a volume. Comparing them shows why bigger things have less surface for their size.

maths.problem: You have about 30 trillion cells. That is 30 followed by 12 zeros. Suppose you could count one cell every second. A year has about 31 million seconds. Roughly how many years would it take to count all your cells?
maths.explain: 30 trillion divided by 31 million is close to 30 million million divided by 30 million, which is about 1 million. So counting one cell a second would take nearly a million years.
maths.context: This problem is about how many cells make up a human body.
maths.why_maths: Very big numbers are hard to feel. Turning them into years makes the size of the number something you can imagine.

maths.problem: In your Hay Pond, suppose a paramecium splits into two once a day, and each new one also splits once a day. You start with 1 paramecium. How many are there after 6 days?
maths.explain: The number doubles each day: 1 becomes 2, then 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64. That is 2 multiplied by itself 6 times.
maths.context: In the Hay Pond project you look for single-celled swimmers that multiply by splitting in two.
maths.why_maths: Doubling is a pattern that grows very fast. Spotting it explains how one cell can fill a jar in a few weeks.

maths.problem: A potato strip weighs 20 grams, and about 80 of every 100 grams of potato is water. How many grams of water are in the strip? If the strip loses one quarter of its water in strong salt water, how many grams of water has it lost?
maths.answer: 16 grams of water, and 4 grams lost.
maths.explain: 80 out of 100 is 80 percent, and 80 percent of 20 grams is 16 grams. A quarter of 16 grams is 4 grams. So the strip loses 4 grams, and weighs about 16 grams after.
maths.context: This problem follows the Potato Strips test, where water leaves the potato cells.
maths.why_maths: Percentages and fractions let you work out how much of a whole is water, and how much leaves it.

maths.problem: A human red blood cell is about 8 micrometres wide. There are 1000 micrometres in 1 millimetre. How many red blood cells would fit side by side across 1 millimetre?
maths.explain: 1000 divided by 8 is 125. So about 125 red blood cells in a line would stretch across 1 millimetre, which is the width of the line a sharp pencil makes.
maths.context: This problem is about how small a red blood cell is.
maths.why_maths: Changing between units lets you picture a size too small to see by comparing it with something you know.

maths.problem: An animal cell is about 20 micrometres wide. You want to build a model of it that is 10 cm wide. How many times bigger than the real cell is your model? Remember that 1 centimetre is 10,000 micrometres.
maths.explain: 10 cm is 100,000 micrometres, because 10 times 10,000 is 100,000. Then 100,000 divided by 20 is 5000. Your model is 5000 times bigger than the real cell.
maths.context: This problem follows the cell models you build, which are much bigger than a real cell.
maths.why_maths: A scale tells you how many times bigger a model is than the real thing, so you can judge sizes in the model fairly.

challenges.title: Be the Membrane: build a filter that picks by size
challenges.problem: Build a filter that lets water and dissolved salt through, but stops rice, sago and sand. Then find out what your filter cannot do that a real cell skin can.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
The filter must be made of a cut plastic bottle with a cloth or paper over the opening.
Test it with the same mix three times.
Do not taste the mix or the water that comes through.
A grown-up cuts the bottle, and smooths the edge with tape. Keep sand and small grains away from small children's mouths.
materials: a clean plastic bottle cut in half by a grown-up to make a funnel
a tea strainer, muslin, a clean cotton cloth, a paper towel and a coffee filter or tissue
a tumbler of water with a teaspoon of salt dissolved in it
a pinch of rice, a pinch of sago (sabudana) and a pinch of sand
a jug or a tall glass to catch the water
a rubber band, tape and a ruler or spoon for stirring
general: Place a paper towel in the funnel. Pour the mix in. The rice, sago and sand stay on the paper, and the salty water goes through.
Stretch muslin over the funnel and hold it with a rubber band. Pour the mix in and see what is left behind.
Layer a tea strainer over a cloth. The strainer stops the rice and sago, and the cloth stops the sand.
creative: Stack three layers, the tea strainer on top, then muslin, then a paper towel. Pour slowly and compare the water at each layer.
Add a few drops of turmeric water to the mix. See that the colour passes right through every filter, while the sand does not.
Make the layers like the skin of a cell, with different holes at different places, and draw which visitors from the Gatekeeper game each layer would stop.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own filter from three layers. Test it with the mix. Then think about this: your filter cannot tell salt from sugar. Why is a real cell skin cleverer than your filter?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the cell membrane. A membrane stops some things and lets others through, and your filter will do something like that using only size.

setup.art: A cut plastic bottle held upside-down in a jug as a funnel, with a paper towel inside and a mix of rice, sago and sand being poured in.
setup.caption: 1. Make a funnel from a cut bottle. Put a paper towel inside.

setup.art: The funnel after pouring: rice, sago and sand left on the paper and clear water dripping into the jug.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the mix in. See what stays on the paper and what goes through.

setup.art: A child with three different cloths and papers laid out and one chosen for the funnel.
setup.caption: 3. Try a different layer. Which one lets only water and salt through?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child what the filter must stop and what it must let through. Ask what in a real cell does a similar job.
flow.say: Your filter must stop rice, sago and sand. It must let water and salt through. What does a similar job in a real cell?
flow.kid: The filter stops rice, sago and sand. It lets water through. Where is a skin like this?

ask.q: What in a cell stops some things and lets others in?

flow.do: Stir the mix and pour it slowly into the filter. Look at what stays on top and what drips through. Try a different layer. Test each layer three times. Write what stays behind and what goes through.
