ask.q: Which layer worked best, and why?
good: The paper towel, because it has the smallest holes.
The muslin, because it let the water go quickly.

flow.parent: With 2-4 children, each child tests a different layer and the group compares. The paper towel stops the sand, rice and sago but is slow. The tea strainer lets fine sand through. Neither stops dissolved salt or turmeric, because they are too small to catch. A real cell skin does stop dissolved salt, with its pumps and channels, and that is the clever part.

check.q: Does your filter stop the salt that is dissolved in the water?
options: No, the dissolved salt goes right through
Yes, the paper catches it
Only if the paper is wet
check.why: Dissolved salt is made of tiny particles, far smaller than the holes in any cloth or paper. Only a real cell skin, with pumps and carriers, can stop dissolved salt. If you picked yes, taste is not a test. You could dry a spoon of the water on a plate in the sun to see crystals.

flow.context: In this step you test your layers. You write what each one stops.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain their best filter. Then ask how a cell's skin is cleverer than the filter.
flow.say: Explain your best filter. Then tell me one thing that a cell skin can do and your filter cannot.
flow.kid: Explain your best filter. What can a cell skin do that it cannot?
flow.think: Your filter picks only by size. A cell skin also picks by what the visitor is made of. How could it do that?
flow.context: This is the last step of Be the Membrane. You explain your design and compare it with a cell skin.

roots.context: We have tested what salt does to the water in a cell, and looked inside a cell at her skin, jelly and instruction room. Now we ask what the cell's edge tells us about being one thing among many.

deep_truth.truth: Potato strips stayed stiff in plain water and went limp in strong salt water. A cell's skin lets water through in both directions. So the water inside a cell depends on the world outside as well as on the cell. A cell is not a sealed bag that decides alone.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a cell, and a body, as a sealed bag with its own fixed contents, and a skin as a wall that shuts the world out. A skin is where a cell and her surroundings trade all the time.
deep_truth.evidence: In the potato strips test, the same strips were stiff or floppy depending only on how much salt was in the water outside. The water that left the strips went into the cup. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You are about thirty trillion cells, and each one trades water and food with the cells and the blood around her. Your body is a place where water keeps coming and going.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing we know is at least one cell. A cell is a pocket with an edge that keeps choosing what comes in and what goes out, for as long as she lives.
three.what_is_this_world: The water in a potato strip, a pickle bowl and a pond all follows the same rule. Water ends up on the side with more dissolved stuff. The same rule works inside a plant and outside it.

roots.thread: A cell has an inside only because she has an edge, and she stays alive only by trading across that edge. Water, air and food pass through her skin every second. The cell you were at the very start came from a cell, in a line of cells going back billions of years. In some of those cells, a bacterium moved into a bigger cell and stayed, and both lived on together. So even one cell is a meeting of many living beings. The cell's edge is the place where many become one and one meets many.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet in the hub of a wheel, but the empty space in the middle makes the wheel useful. Clay is shaped into a pot, but the empty space inside makes the pot useful.
teachings.link: A cell is also a shape that makes an inside. Her skin makes a space where chemistry can happen, and the space is what makes her a cell.

teachings.source: Isha Upanishad, opening verse (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1)
teachings.teaching: 'That is whole, this is whole. From the whole the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.'
teachings.link: A single cell, such as an amoeba, splits into two. Each new cell is a whole cell, and nothing has been taken away from the first.

teachings.teaching: Margulis argued that life has grown as much by living things joining together as by competing. She showed that mitochondria began as free-living bacteria that moved into other cells.
teachings.link: Each of your cells holds the descendants of bacteria that became partners. A cell is a community.

science.text: Fat molecules put into water form hollow bubbles on their own, and these bubbles have been shown in laboratories to hold chemicals inside. This is one reason scientists think the skin could have appeared early.
Whether the first cell began with a skin, with instructions or with chemistry is still not known.

other_view.view: A cell's skin is a piece of chemistry. Fat molecules, proteins and pumps follow physical rules, and nothing decides. Saying a cell chooses what comes in is a short way of describing the pumps and channels working.

how_we_found_out.story: By the 1800s, scientists could see the stiff walls around plant cells. But the thin skin around the living jelly inside was far too thin for any microscope. Some scientists said it was not there at all, and that the jelly simply stopped. In 1877, Wilhelm Pfeffer, a German plant scientist, measured how strongly water is pulled through a man-made skin. Plant scientists such as Hugo de Vries saw plant cells shrink away from their walls in strong solutions. A living skin that lets water through must be there, they said, though nobody could see it. In the 1890s, Ernest Overton found that substances that dissolve in fat get into cells fastest, so the skin must be fatty. In 1925, a Dutch children's doctor named Evelyn Gorter and her colleague François Grendel spread out the fat from red blood cells on water. It covered about twice the surface of the cells, so the skin had two layers. Their measurements were rough. Electron microscopes in the 1950s finally showed the skin, with two layers.
how_we_found_out.who: Wilhelm Pfeffer, Ernest Overton, and Evelyn Gorter with François Grendel
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Some scientists thought a cell had no skin and that the jelly simply stopped. Water and dissolved stuff moved in a way only a skin could explain, and the skin was finally seen with an electron microscope.

Potato Strips: the strip sizes, the 1 and 4 teaspoons of salt in 200 millilitres and the times of 20 and 40 minutes are from the usual home version of this test. The droop numbers in the notes (a few millimetres for plain water, much more for strong salt water) are what such tests usually give, so a family's own numbers may differ, and the steps say what to do if all the strips stay stiff. Naked Egg: the shell takes one to two days to dissolve in vinegar, the size changes are usually a centimetre or so, and the step notes say how to handle raw egg. Families who avoid raw egg can skip it. Limp to Crisp, Raisin Swell and Ice Race use things in every kitchen, but the minutes given for the herb standing up and the ice melting depend on how warm the kitchen is. Hay Pond may show only cloudy water and tiny moving specks, not clear shapes, and the step notes say so. The cell models and the filter challenge are food and household things only. Two games are written as paper games with cards to cut out, and both can be played alone. The videos have no address yet.
